## The London Choral Service When the music has to be perfect

Professional singers, choirs, and instrumentalists for funerals, weddings, memorials, and ceremonies across the United Kingdom. A small, hand-picked team chosen and directed by an Oxford-trained Artistic Director.

Musicians from the Royal Academy, the Royal College, and Britain’s leading conservatoires.


### The right music for the moment

A single voice to hold a room in stillness. A four-part choir to carry a congregation through a hymn. A twelve-voice chorus with strings to fill a cathedral. We match the ensemble to the venue, the congregation, and the music you want.

You tell us what you need, or we help you decide. We handle rehearsals, repertoire, and logistics, so the music on the day is one less thing for you to think about.

### Christmas 2026

In December our choirs sing carol services in offices, livery halls, and churches, and our carol singers work hotel lobbies, drinks receptions, and residents’ evenings — roaming among guests or singing sets, entirely a cappella if the space has no piano. We charge the same rates in December as the rest of the year, and the popular dates are usually gone by mid-September.

### Who we are

Every musician has been personally chosen by Artistic Director Luca Wetherall (Tutor in Music, University of Oxford) for their voice and for how they carry themselves at a funeral or a wedding. Graduates of the Royal Academy of Music, the Royal College of Music, and Britain's leading music colleges.

Their credits include the coronation of King Charles III, the Olympics closing ceremony, the Royal Albert Hall, Westminster Abbey, and St Paul's Cathedral. They perform with the BBC Proms, the Royal Philharmonic, and the English National Opera. They read a room and adjust on the day — softer when a family is struggling, stronger when a congregation needs carrying through a hymn.

## About our musicians

We put the right singers in the right building, prepared and rehearsed, for the occasion you are planning.


### Our story

Luca Wetherall founded The London Choral Service after years of directing music at ceremonies and seeing the same problem: families wanted live music but had no reliable way to find trained singers at short notice. He built a small team of conservatoire-trained musicians who could be trusted to arrive prepared, know the building, and lead the music without needing to be managed.

Luca studied music at the University of Oxford, where he now holds a position as Tutor in Music. He auditions every singer and instrumentalist on the team himself. That selectiveness is the foundation of the service. When you book with us, you are booking musicians Luca has heard and chosen.

“Luca understood straight away what we needed. He suggested pieces we’d never have found on our own, and the singers were faultless.”

A hymn sung with conviction carries a congregation through their grief or joy. A solo voice can hold a room so still you can hear a hymn book close at the back. A full choir in a large church produces a sound you feel in your chest.

We match you with the right musicians, plan the repertoire with you, and handle rehearsals, sheet music, and venue liaison. On the day, the music is one less thing for you to think about.


### Our musicians

We keep the team small on purpose. Luca selects for two things: a voice that can carry a building, and the awareness to hold back when the occasion calls for it. Technique alone is not enough when a family is grieving or a couple is exchanging vows.

Our musicians are prize-winning graduates of the Royal Academy of Music, the Royal College of Music, the Guildhall School of Music & Drama, and the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge. Their credits include the coronation of King Charles III, the Olympics closing ceremony, the BBC Proms, the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, the English National Opera, the Royal Albert Hall, Westminster Abbey, St Paul’s Cathedral, and the Royal Opera House.

What matters most: they arrive understanding that the ceremony belongs to the people in the room, not to the performers. Listen to recordings of our musicians .

“Our guests kept saying the music was the highlight. The choir sang during the signing of the register and you could hear a pin drop. Perfect.”

We hold diary space for short-notice work, because most families are not booking weeks ahead. We offer vocal ensembles from a single soloist to a twelve-voice chorus, plus keyboard and string players. See our full range of services , or browse our music guides for help choosing repertoire.


### Where we perform

Based in London, available nationwide. We have performed at Westminster Abbey, St Paul’s Cathedral, Southwark Cathedral, Brompton Oratory, Temple Church, the Guards’ Chapel, St Martin-in-the-Fields, and Chelsea Old Church. We perform just as often in parish churches and crematoriums across the UK, from London to Oxford , Birmingham , and Manchester . See all areas .

If you already have a venue, we recommend the ideal ensemble size and instrumentation for the space. If you are still deciding, we are happy to advise. Luca knows the acoustics of hundreds of churches and ceremony venues across London and the South East. Our pricing page sets out clearly what each ensemble option costs.

For ceremonies outside the UK, our performing ensemble Alma Consort takes a small number of private and international engagements each year.


### How we work

It starts with a conversation. Tell us about the occasion, the venue, and the mood you have in mind. If you have music in mind, we will talk about it. If you are unsure, we will guide you — a short conversation usually settles the repertoire.

We then send a recommendation — the ensemble, the repertoire, the programme order — with a written quote. Once you confirm, we handle rehearsals, sheet music, and coordination with your venue or funeral director. You will not need to chase us or manage logistics.

On the day, our musicians arrive early, set up quietly, and perform the programme you agreed.

“I rang up not really knowing what I wanted and she couldn’t have been kinder. The quartet were outstanding. Several people have asked me for the details since.”

### Our ensembles

Every booking includes one to three performance pieces and leading the congregation in all of the hymns. The chorus performs up to four pieces.

- Soloist One voice One trained singer, suited to smaller chapels and crematoriums where the voice sits close to the congregation.
- Small Choir 4 singers Soprano, alto, tenor, and bass in four-part harmony. Fills a church seating 50 to 200 without overpowering the room.
- Quintet 5 singers A second soprano makes a real difference to the sound and opens up the repertoire. Helps lead the congregation more confidently.
- Sextet 6 singers Six voices produce a bigger sound than a quartet at a price well below a full choir. Suits mid-to-large churches.
- Full Choir 8 singers Eight voices carry to the back of a large church or cathedral and split into eight-part harmony for Stanford or Parry.
- Chorus 12 singers Twelve voices fill a cathedral and handle complex works that smaller groups cannot attempt, from Fauré to large-scale anthems.
Pianists, organists, harpists, and string quartets perform alongside our singers or on their own. We match the instrumentation to your venue, your repertoire, and whether the music is sacred, classical, or contemporary.

### Where we perform

We perform in parish churches, cathedrals, crematoriums, chapels, synagogues, hotels, private homes, gardens, marquees, concert halls, and outdoor spaces. If your venue has specific acoustic or logistical needs, Luca will advise on the right ensemble size and setup.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What types of occasions do you provide music for?

We provide live music for funerals, weddings, memorials, celebrations of life, corporate events, and ceremonies of all kinds across the United Kingdom. That includes religious services, civil ceremonies, humanist celebrations, and private gatherings. If your occasion does not fit a standard category, get in touch. We have performed at naming ceremonies, anniversary services, charity galas, and school events.


#### What ensemble sizes are available?

We offer a soloist (single voice), quartet (4 singers), quintet (5 singers), sextet (6 singers), full choir (8 singers), and chorus (12 singers). We also provide organists, pianists, harpists, and string quartets. The right ensemble depends on your venue size, your budget, and the sound you want. A soloist suits an intimate crematorium chapel. A full choir fills a large parish church. Luca will recommend the best option when you get in touch.


#### How quickly can you respond?

Most enquiries get a reply from Luca within 48 hours, often the same day. We have arranged singers at a few hours’ notice when families had no other option. If your service is in the next 48 hours, call us on 07356 042468 — email may not be fast enough.


#### Can you arrange any piece of music?

Our repertoire spans classical, sacred, and contemporary music. If there is a piece you want to hear, whether it is a Bach chorale, a folk song, or a pop ballad, we can arrange it for your chosen ensemble. Luca will quote for the arrangement up front, and send you a recording of it before the day so you can hear how it sounds. The only limitation is copyright: some publishers restrict live performance of certain works, but this affects very few pieces.

## Hear our singers and musicians

A selection of the pieces our clients request most often, performed by our singers and instrumentalists.


### Most requested


#### Abide With Me — Full Choir

One of the most beloved funeral hymns in the English tradition. The four-part harmonies carry a congregation through a hymn most people in the room will already know.


#### He Shall Feed His Flock — Soloist, from Handel’s Messiah

One of the most tender and consoling arias in all of Handel's Messiah. Gentle, unhurried, and peaceful — a beautiful choice for a funeral or memorial service.


#### Be Thou My Vision — Full Choir

An eighth-century Irish text sung to the folk melody Slane. Especially beautiful in a choral setting with organ accompaniment.


#### Ubi Caritas — Full Choir, Ola Gjeilo

A modern setting of the Latin antiphon “where charity and love are, God is there.” Sung unaccompanied. One of the most requested pieces at weddings and funerals alike — read why it suits a wedding .


#### Anima Christi — Marco Frisina

A fourteenth-century Latin prayer set by Monsignor Marco Frisina of the Diocese of Rome, sung here by a quintet with one soprano on the melody. Catholic families ask for it at Nuptial Masses and Requiems alike, and a soloist with an organist carries it equally well. Read our guides to Anima Christi at a Catholic wedding and at a Catholic funeral .


#### Ave Maria — Soloist

Schubert's beloved setting — by far the most requested piece across all our services. Traditionally performed by a solo soprano.


#### How Great Thou Art — Full Choir

A hymn of tremendous power. The choral harmonies build gradually, culminating in one of the most stirring climaxes in all congregational music.


#### Ave Verum Corpus — Full Choir

Mozart's sublime motet — four minutes of stillness, written in the last weeks of his life. Many musicians consider it the most perfect short piece of choral music there is.


#### The Lord's My Shepherd — Small Choir

The most chosen hymn at funerals across the United Kingdom, sung here to the Crimond melody. Gentle and familiar, and a hymn most congregations sing without needing the words.


#### Amazing Grace — Soloist

Perhaps the world’s best-known hymn. It carries just as well sung by one voice as by a full choir.


#### Jerusalem — Full Choir

Parry's magnificent setting of Blake's visionary poem. A favourite at weddings, memorials, and national occasions — thrilling with a full choir and organ.


### Something different


#### Blue Christmas — Small Choir

The Elvis number, sung in harmony. We put it between the traditional carols at drinks receptions and office parties. Most years our December dates go by the middle of September, so see Christmas carol services or hire carol singers .


#### Fields of Gold — Soloist

Sting's gentle, luminous ballad. Perfectly suited to a solo voice with piano accompaniment — reflective and warm, without being sad. A beautiful choice for celebrations of life.


#### Somewhere Over the Rainbow — Soloist

It speaks to hope and yearning without demanding sadness. Disarmingly simple, and often chosen to capture someone's optimism or adventurous spirit.


#### In Paradisum — Small Choir

The closing movement of the Fauré Requiem — which never rises above a hush. One of the most beautiful pieces in the choral repertoire.


#### Danny Boy — Soloist

The Irish air, set to the Londonderry melody, sung with warmth and restraint.


#### Time to Say Goodbye — Soloist

Unmistakable from the first bars. A bold choice that makes a statement at a celebration of life.


### Hymns


#### Make Me a Channel of Your Peace — Small Choir

The prayer of St Francis, set to a gentle, singable melody that congregations find easy to join in with.


#### Guide Me, O Thou Great Redeemer — Full Choir

The great Welsh hymn, sung to Cwm Rhondda. Written for a congregation in full voice, and it works exactly that way at a service.


#### All Things Bright and Beautiful — Small Choir

A hymn that celebrates the natural world. Particularly well suited to celebrations of life and outdoor services.

“We’d listened to a few recordings online but nothing prepared us for hearing them in person. Four voices and it filled the entire chapel. People were in tears.”

This is a sample of what we offer. If there is a piece you have imagined hearing at your occasion, whether classical, sacred, contemporary, or something further afield, we can almost certainly perform it. We also write bespoke arrangements when the piece you want does not exist in a form that suits your ensemble.

For help choosing the right pieces, explore our funeral music guide or wedding hymns guide .

## Choir and singer pricing

Last updated: August 2026

Flat prices, all in. What you see is what you pay — no hidden fees, no surprises. Prices include all fees and taxes. Travel costs may apply for venues beyond Greater London.


### Choirs & singers

Book a soloist or choir together with an organist or pianist and the accompaniment costs less than booking it separately.

- Soloist with an organist or pianist: £450, instead of £500 booked apart.
- Organist or pianist added to any choir: £225, below the £250 standalone rate.

### Christmas & carol singers

Christmas bookings are charged at the table rates above, and carol bookings start with a Small Choir of four, since the singing is normally unaccompanied. A soloist is available for a sung grace or a single set piece at a dinner. A carol service in an office, livery hall, or hired church, or carol singers roaming a party or singing sets in a lobby, costs the same as the equivalent ensemble at any other time of year. Prices include all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London.

A standard Christmas booking covers up to an hour and a half including breaks, or the length of a church service. The choir sings entirely a cappella where there is no instrument, and we can also provide an organist or pianist, or background piano between sets. Bringing a keyboard and speaker to a venue without a piano carries an extra charge, quoted upfront. Christmas Eve and Christmas Day dates carry a premium of around 25%, and December diaries usually close by mid-September. Our carol singers cost guide breaks down the options.

### Frequently asked questions


#### What are the standard rates for funeral music?

A solo funeral singer starts from £250. A small choir of four singers costs from £1,150, a quintet from £1,400, a sextet from £1,600, a full choir of eight from £2,000, and a twelve-voice chorus from £3,000. All prices include fees and taxes. The same rates apply for weddings, memorials, and other ceremonies. Our popular funeral hymns guide can help you decide what music to include.


#### Are there any hidden fees?

No. The price we quote is the price you pay. All fees and taxes are included. Travel costs may apply for venues outside Greater London, but we discuss those upfront before you commit. You will never receive an unexpected invoice.


#### Do prices include travel?

Prices shown cover venues within Greater London. For venues further afield, travel costs depend on the location and the number of singers. We calculate the travel supplement before you book and include it in your written quote, so you know the full cost from the start.


#### Can I get a custom quote?

Yes. Get in touch with the date, venue, and any details about the occasion. We will send a written quote within 48 hours. There is no obligation and no charge for the quote itself.


#### Can you provide music at short notice?

Yes. We regularly arrange funeral music at short notice, sometimes within 48 hours. Contact us with your date and we will confirm availability the same day. For weddings and other planned events, we recommend booking at least six months ahead.


#### Do your prices go up at Christmas?

No. December bookings are charged at the same rates as the rest of the year, inclusive of taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. The exceptions are Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, which carry a premium of around 25%, confirmed in your written quote before you book.


#### How long does a Christmas carol booking last?

A standard Christmas booking covers up to an hour and a half including breaks, or the length of a church carol service. Longer programmes are possible for a premium fee, quoted upfront. Between sets we can provide background piano if your venue has an instrument.

Published 18 August 2026

If you are comparing quotes for funeral singers in London, you are doing it in a week with a great deal else to arrange. This page sets out what The London Funeral Singers charge, what we charge, and what each price covers.


### The gap is wider than it looks

The London Funeral Singers quote before VAT, so the printed price is not the invoice price. The table below shows both figures next to ours, which already include travel inside Greater London.

### How much singing you get

Price is half the comparison. The other half is how much music the price buys.


### Who sings

We keep the team small on purpose. Luca Wetherall, our Artistic Director and a Tutor in Music at the University of Oxford, auditions every singer himself and picks the ensemble for your service.

Our quartets and sextets rehearse and sing together rather than coming together for a single booking. That is what lets four voices fill a parish church without straining.

### Frequently asked questions


#### Why are your prices lower?

We are not VAT-registered, so nothing is added at the end. We keep a small team rather than a large agency book. Travel within Greater London, sheet music, and rehearsal are already in the quoted figure.


#### Do you charge VAT?

No. Your invoice comes from Alma Consort Ltd, the operating company behind The London Choral Service. It is not VAT-registered, so the price we quote is the price you pay.


#### What is included in the price?

Rehearsal and preparation, sheet music, a music director, coordination with your funeral director and the venue, and travel within Greater London.


#### How many pieces will the choir sing?

Up to three performance pieces plus every hymn in the service, for any ensemble from four singers to eight. A twelve-voice chorus covers up to four pieces.


#### Can you arrange singers at short notice?

Yes. We hold diary space for short-notice work. A 48-hour turnaround is normal and shorter is often possible.

### Wedding music questions


#### When in the ceremony does the choir sing?

A choir can sing as guests arrive, during the processional, at the signing of the register, and for the recessional, as well as leading the hymns. #### Can you perform a song that isn't a traditional hymn?

Yes. Alongside hymns and classical repertoire, we arrange pop songs, musical-theatre numbers, and folk pieces for our voices. If a song means something to you, send it over and we will tell you how it works for the ensemble you have in mind.


#### Do you sing with our church's organist, or bring your own?

Either. Where a church has its own organist we sing with them; where it does not, or theirs is unavailable, we bring an organist who has played that instrument. Adding an organist to a choir is £225.


#### How many singers do we need for our venue?

Four voices fill most parish churches and give you full harmony; six or eight suit a cathedral or a long guest list. We advise once we know the building and the numbers. Our wedding choir guide walks through the options.

## Christmas carol services Professional choirs for companies, venues, and churches

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

Offices and companies book us first: the annual carol service, the gala dinner, the client drinks reception. The same choirs sing in hotels, at residents’ Christmas evenings, in livery halls, at charity carol concerts, and at private parties. Carol bookings start with four voices in full harmony, and run up to twelve, unaccompanied or with an organist.

This page covers structured carol services and concerts. If you want singers moving through a party or a lobby instead, hire carol singers .

Trusted by law firms, banks, charities, and City livery companies. Musicians from the Royal Academy, Royal College, and Britain’s leading conservatoires.

Tell us about your event

### How it works


#### Tell us about your event

Share the date, venue, format, and any preferences. We send a proposal within 48 hours.


#### We plan the programme

#### We perform

### What we provide

A carol service, a gala dinner, a drinks reception, and an office party each want a different shape. A carol service usually calls for a full choir of eight with an organist. A drinks reception works better with four singers alternating traditional carols and a cappella arrangements of popular Christmas songs. A formal dinner may need one voice for a sung grace and a single set piece.

Where the singing happens changes the answer as much as the occasion does. In a hotel lobby or an atrium, three or four short sets across an evening suit the flow of guests better than one long concert. At a residents’ Christmas evening, a song sheet and four carols the whole building can join in on does more than a recital. A livery hall wants a sung grace and a short formal set before the loving cup; a ticketed charity concert wants a printed order of service and readers between the carols.

Luca Wetherall, our Artistic Director, discusses your event with you or your event coordinator, then sends a proposal with ensemble options and a programme outline. We handle all coordination with your venue or event manager. Our musicians arrive in concert dress, set up without fuss, and perform to the brief. If you would rather they wore all black, ordinary clothes, or Christmas jumpers, say so and they will.

Beyond the music, we can help organise the wider event. We assist with finding and booking a venue, printing programmes, and arranging refreshments — so you can hand off as much or as little of the planning as you like.

Our clients include law firms, banks, charities, schools, and City livery companies across London and the UK.

For company Christmas parties, awards dinners, and year-round corporate events, see also our corporate music page .

“We hire the London Choral Service for our annual carol service every December. The choir knows the building, the format, and exactly what we need. Our partners and clients look forward to it each year.”

“The choir were the highlight of our Christmas drinks. They moved through the crowd singing carols and it completely transformed the atmosphere. Several clients have already asked if we’re doing it again next year.”


### Carol services in churches

Companies, charities, and livery companies often book a church for an evening in December and then need musicians to fill it. You settle the date with the incumbent; we supply the choir and, where the building has a decent instrument, an organist who has played it before. If the church has no organist of its own, or theirs is already committed that week, ours covers the hymns, the carols, and the voluntaries at either end.

The first thing we agree is which carols the congregation sings and which the choir takes alone. Four singers will lead a room of 150 through Hark! The Herald Angels Sing ; eight will carry a church of 400. In between those, the choir sings the pieces a congregation cannot: the Willcocks descants, Poston’s Jesus Christ the Apple Tree , an unaccompanied Gaudete . Six of each is the usual balance for an hour.

The running order is yours to choose. A liturgical service follows the Nine Lessons and Carols pattern from King’s College: a bidding prayer, nine readings from scripture, a carol after each, a blessing at the end. A secular running order drops the prayers and puts a chief executive, a patron, or a beneficiary in the reading slots instead, usually with the appeal placed before the last carol. Either runs to about an hour.

We deal with the building direct. Vergers control access, heating, lighting, and how long you get in the church before the doors open; clergy will want to see the order of service if any liturgy is involved. We contact them once the booking is confirmed and send you the arrival and rehearsal times rather than asking you to broker it.

Accompaniment is a separate decision from the size of the choir. The singers can perform a cappella throughout, which needs no instrument and no amplification and is the usual answer in offices and hotel lobbies. In a church we would normally send an organist, added to any choir for £225. At a reception or a party, a pianist can support the singing, or we can send a choir with background piano between the sets, where the pianist covers the gaps and the singers come back in for each set. If the venue has no piano at all, we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in your written quote.

### Frequently asked questions


#### How late can we book a choir for a carol service in December?

Most years our December dates go by the middle of September, and the first three weeks of the month are the tightest. We do take later bookings when the right combination of singers is still free, so it is always worth asking. Send us the date and we will confirm availability the same day.


#### What music does the choir sing at a Christmas carol service?

All the traditional carols, from Once in Royal David’s City to O Holy Night, and a cappella arrangements of popular Christmas songs for receptions and parties. Luca builds the programme around your running order and marks which carols the room sings and which the choir takes alone.


#### Can the choir roam around the venue or sing outdoors?

Both work. The singers can move through a lobby, a drinks reception, or a switch-on crowd, or stay in one position for set pieces. Dress is your call: concert dress, all black, casual, or Christmas jumpers, and we have Santa hats if you want them.


#### What happens if the venue has no piano or organ?

Nothing changes. The choir sings a cappella and needs no instrument and no amplification. If you would rather have keyboard accompaniment, we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in your written quote so there is no surprise on the invoice.


#### How much does a Christmas carol service cost?

We charge no Christmas uplift, so the standard prices apply. A Small Choir of four is £1,150, a sextet £1,600, a full choir of eight £2,000, and a chorus of twelve £3,000, inclusive of all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. A standard booking runs up to 1.5 hours including breaks, or the length of a church service; longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront. Full pricing is on our pricing page .


#### Are you available on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day?

Yes, we sing on both, including carols by candlelight on the 24th. Those two dates carry a premium, typically around 25 per cent, confirmed in the written quote before you commit to anything. They are the first dates to go each year, so ask early.


#### Can you sing a carol service in a church we have booked?

Yes. You arrange the church and the date with the incumbent, and we bring the choir and, if you want the carols accompanied, an organist who knows the instrument in that building. We deal with the clergy and vergers direct on rehearsal access, seating, and the running order.

Three to six months ahead is the ideal lead time, especially for popular dates between May and September. Shorter timelines work too. We can usually confirm a quartet within a week if the date is clear, and we have rescued more than one wedding when the previous musicians fell through three weeks out.

You stay in the loop on whatever cadence suits you. Some planners want every email copied; some want a single sign-off when the running order is finalised; some want us to handle everything and only call them if there is a problem. Tell us what works and we follow your lead.


### What your couples receive

A direct conversation with Luca, who has worked on hundreds of weddings. He listens to the couple and suggests music that fits both the venue and the tone of the day. Couples who arrive saying “we have no idea what music to have” leave the call with a complete plan they are excited about.

We’re happy to do custom arrangements, but this may result in an extra charge depending on the specific requirements. If a couple wants a Bach chorale, a pop song, a hymn arranged for a small ensemble, or a piece their grandparents played at their own wedding, we arrange it for the chosen voices and rehearse it before the day. Recordings of the suggested arrangements go to the couple before they commit.

A confirmed running order goes to you and the couple a week before the wedding. It lists every piece, every position in the ceremony, who is performing it, and how long it lasts. The officiant gets a copy. We rehearse with the organist, if there is one, by phone in advance.

“We had no idea what music to choose and Luca made it so easy. He sent us recordings of every piece and we planned the whole ceremony over two short calls. On the day it was seamless.”


### On the day

Musicians arrive an hour before the ceremony. They introduce themselves to your team, find their position with the officiant, run through any cues with the wedding party, and set up quietly without disturbing guests as they arrive.

Technical needs are minimal. For most ceremonies all we need is a small clear space for the singers to stand and good acoustic visibility to where the couple will exchange vows. If the venue has no piano or organ and the couple wants accompaniment, we bring a portable keyboard and need one standard 13-amp socket within ten metres. For outdoor ceremonies, we discuss whether light amplification is needed in advance.

After the ceremony, we can continue through drinks and the wedding breakfast if the couple wants a single musical thread running through the whole day. A jazz trio over canapés, a string quartet during the meal, or a sextet leading guests in singing — whatever fits the brief.

“Our guests kept saying the music was the highlight. The choir sang during the signing of the register and you could hear a pin drop. Perfect.”

Transparent, published pricing the couple can budget against. Every booking includes the music consultation with Luca, a written running order, and on-the-day coordination. Custom arrangements are available; depending on the specific requirements, they may add to the fee.

## The sound of an English cathedral, wherever you are.

A professional consort of eight to twenty-four voices, travelling from London to sing weddings, memorials, private concerts, and ceremonies of state and celebration in Europe, North America, and the Gulf.

Enquire about your event

The ensemble


### The ensemble

The London Choral Service is the booking office of Alma Consort, a professional ensemble of consort singers based in London. The same singers perform every engagement.

The singers are prize-winning graduates of the Royal Academy of Music, the Royal College of Music, the Guildhall School of Music & Drama, and the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge. Their credits include the coronation of King Charles III, the BBC Proms, Westminster Abbey, St Paul’s Cathedral, the Royal Opera House, and the English National Opera. Luca Wetherall, Tutor in Music at the University of Oxford, directs the consort and auditions every singer himself.

The ensemble’s own site is almaconsort.com .

Voicing


### Choosing a voicing

Alma Consort sings in four sizes, and the right one depends on the building and the number of guests.

Twelve voices give two singers to each part, with four soloists besides. This is our recommendation for most churches: enough sound for the nave, and a solo voice free to step forward for an Ave Maria or a solo verse.

Alma Consort in performance.

Repertoire


### Repertoire

We sing sacred and secular music, with the English tradition at its core: Byrd and Tallis through Parry and Howells, alongside plainsong, European polyphony, and contemporary settings. For a reception, a dinner, or a private concert we sing part-songs and folk arrangements, and we arrange songs written for other forces — if a piece matters to you and no choral setting exists, we will make one or commission it.

The consort sings unaccompanied or with an organist; we can also bring instrumentalists where the programme asks for them. Luca Wetherall plans the whole programme with you, around the occasion and the building.


#### Where we have sung

We sing at private events in churches, chapels, hotels, country houses, and private estates, and we travel internationally, including across Europe and the United States. In London, our singers have performed at:

- Westminster Abbey
- St Paul’s Cathedral
- Southwark Cathedral
- Brompton Oratory
- Temple Church
- the Guards’ Chapel
- St Martin-in-the-Fields
- Chelsea Old Church

Planners & venues


### For planners and venues

We work with event and wedding planners, private offices, and the events teams of luxury hotels and estates. We hold public liability insurance and can provide risk assessments and method statements. We invoice in pounds sterling, euros, or US dollars.

Questions


### Private engagement questions


#### Where do you travel?

Anywhere the flights and the rehearsal schedule allow. Europe is the most straightforward: the consort can fly out on a Friday and sing on the Saturday, which is why Italy, France, Ireland, and Scotland come up most often for weddings and country-house ceremonies. We also travel to North America and the Gulf. If your venue is somewhere else, ask us and we will tell you what the calendar allows.


#### How far ahead should we book?

Six to twelve months is usual, and dates abroad want the longer end of that: booking flights and rooms for twelve to twenty-four people takes longer than clearing the singers’ diaries. A date six weeks out is still worth asking about if it happens to be free. Tell us your date as soon as it is fixed, even if the music is nowhere near settled.


#### What determines the cost?

The number of singers, the distance they travel, and the nights they stay. Our UK rates for each ensemble size are published on the pricing page . An engagement abroad also carries return flights and accommodation for the whole consort, who arrive the day before to rehearse in the building. We quote for the whole engagement before you commit, and we invoice in pounds sterling, euros, or US dollars.


#### What do you need from the venue?

Room for the consort to stand where the guests can hear them, which in a church usually means the chancel, a gallery, or the west end. A stone building needs no amplification. For a ballroom or a marquee, send us the dimensions and tell us whether the floor is carpeted: a soft room absorbs sound that a chapel would carry, and that changes the number of singers we recommend.


#### What happens if a singer falls ill?

Luca books the replacement himself, from singers the consort already works with, and briefs them on the programme before they travel. A deputy signs the same confidentiality agreement as everyone else on the engagement.


#### Do you sing outside churches, and beyond sacred music?

Yes to both. At receptions, private dinners, and concerts in country houses and hotels we sing part-songs, folk arrangements, and pieces we arrange for the consort from songs written for other forces. Sacred repertoire suits a memorial or a ceremony of state. Luca builds each programme around the occasion and the building rather than working from a set list.

## Hire carol singers Professional singers for parties, receptions, and December events

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Singers who arrive, sing carols where your guests are already standing, and leave you to run the rest of the evening. Bookings start with four voices and run up to twelve, sung unaccompanied, in offices, hotels, apartment lobbies, at switch-ons and markets, and at parties at home. London and across the UK.

This page covers hiring singers for a party, a reception, or a lobby. If you are planning a full service with readings and congregational carols, see Christmas carol services .

Musicians from the Royal Academy, Royal College, and Britain’s leading conservatoires.

Tell us about your event


### How it works


#### Send us the date and the venue

Tell us when, where, roughly how many guests, and what the singers are meant to be doing. We come back with ensemble options and a written quote within 48 hours.


#### We build the sets

Luca chooses the carols, sets the running order, and agrees positioning, timings, and access with your venue or building manager.


#### The singers arrive and sing

They turn up in the dress you asked for, need nothing but somewhere to stand, and sing to the brief.


### Where carol singers work

Most December bookings are office receptions and staff parties, where four singers work the room as people arrive and the drinks go round. Hotels book us for lobbies and festive afternoon teas. Towns and shopping streets book us for light switch-ons and Christmas markets. Managing agents book us for residents’ evenings and community events in apartment buildings, and families book us for parties at home.

The singers can roam through the crowd, stopping wherever a group has gathered, or stay in one position for sets of three or four carols. Roaming suits a drinks reception where guests arrive across an hour. Stationary sets suit a seated dinner, or a switch-on with a countdown to sing up to.

Everything is sung a cappella, so there is no stage to build, no power to find, and no PA to hire. Give the group a corner of a lobby or the foot of a staircase and they will fill the space. Outdoors is fine as well: markets, courtyards, and switch-ons are ordinary December work, though we will ask for cover from rain and somewhere warm to wait between sets.

Dress is your call. Concert dress for a formal evening, all black for a lobby set that should not draw the eye, ordinary clothes for a market, or Christmas jumpers if you want the singers to look like part of the party. We have Santa hats if you want them. You may know them as carollers (or carolers, in the American spelling); either way it is the same trained group.

The repertoire runs from the traditional carols everyone knows — Ding Dong Merrily on High , Silent Night , Hark! The Herald Angels Sing — through the quieter Advent pieces to a cappella arrangements of the popular Christmas songs people expect at a party. Tell us the tone you are after and Luca sets the running order against it.

We are based in London, and that is where most of the work sits: office lobbies in the City, hotels in Mayfair, receptions in Canary Wharf, residents’ evenings in the riverside buildings. We travel for the rest of the country too. Travel within Greater London is included in the price, and anything further is quoted with the booking.

Where the venue has a piano, you can book the choir with background piano between the sets: the pianist keeps the room from falling silent while the singers rest, then drops out as they come back in. If there is no piano, we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in your written quote. Neither is necessary. The singing stands on its own.

“The choir were the highlight of our Christmas drinks. They moved through the crowd singing carols and it completely transformed the atmosphere. Several clients have already asked if we’re doing it again next year.”

Some of the people who book carol singers have a page of their own, covering what each one asks about first.

#### Blue Christmas — Small Choir

The Elvis number, sung in harmony. Popular at office parties and drinks receptions, where it breaks up a set of traditional carols.

An eighth-century Irish text sung to the folk melody Slane. Especially beautiful in a choral setting with organ accompaniment.


#### Guide Me, O Thou Great Redeemer — Full Choir

The great Welsh hymn, sung to Cwm Rhondda. Written for a congregation in full voice, and it works exactly that way at a service.


#### All Things Bright and Beautiful — Small Choir

A hymn that celebrates the natural world. A favourite at carol services and seasonal gatherings.

### Frequently asked questions


#### How long do carol singers perform for?

A standard Christmas booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks. That is usually three sets of twenty minutes or so, or continuous singing across a shorter reception. Longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront. Where the venue has a piano, a pianist can cover the gaps between the sets.


#### Do carol singers need microphones or amplification?

No. Trained voices carry a hotel lobby or a full office floor unamplified, so there is no stage to build, no PA to hire, and nothing to plug in. Put the singers where the ceiling is high and the floor is hard, such as a staircase, an atrium, or a gallery, and the sound reaches the whole room.


#### How many carol singers should we book for our venue?

Size the group to the space. Four singers suit a lobby, an office reception, or a room of up to 150. Six fill a busy hotel foyer or a mid-sized hall. Eight cover a large hall or a church of 400, and twelve are for several hundred guests or a ticketed concert.


#### Can guests sing along or request a carol?

Yes to both. Song sheets on the well-known carols turn the last ten minutes into a singalong, which works particularly well at residents’ evenings and family parties. Requests are welcome where they sit within the repertoire. Send them a week or two ahead and Luca will place them in the sets.


#### Can carol singers perform outdoors in the cold?

Yes. Markets, courtyards, and light switch-ons are ordinary December work. We ask for cover from rain, since sheet music and wind do not mix, and somewhere warm to wait between sets. In hard frost we sing shorter sets more often rather than standing out for a solid hour.


#### What do carol singers wear?

Whatever suits your event. Concert dress for a formal evening, all black for a lobby set that should not draw the eye, ordinary clothes for a market or a family party, or Christmas jumpers if you want the singers to look festive. Santa hats are available if you ask for them.

#### What kind of carol performance works in an apartment lobby or courtyard?

Both spaces work without any technical setup. In a lobby the singers can roam as residents come in from the lifts and the front door, or stand in one place for a set of carols. Outdoors in a courtyard, at a light switch-on for instance, we sing stationary sets, because a moving choir is harder to hear in open air. We sing a cappella either way, so the building supplies no power, stage, or amplification.


#### Can residents join in and sing, or do the singers perform on their own?

Either, and most residents’ evenings work best as a mix. Print song sheets and we will lead the carols everyone half-remembers from the front; four trained voices are enough to carry a lobby full of people. Alongside that we programme two or three a cappella arrangements that the choir performs while residents listen. Tell us which way you want the evening to lean and we build the programme around it.


#### How does invoicing work for a managing agent?

#### How long does a residents’ carol evening run?

A standard Christmas booking runs up to an hour and a half including the singers’ breaks, which covers most residents’ evenings: long enough for people to drift down over half an hour and still hear a full programme. Longer bookings are possible at a premium, quoted upfront in the written quote so nothing arrives on the invoice you have not already seen.


#### When do we need to book carol singers for a December residents’ event?

December closes out by mid‑September, and the second and third weeks go first. If your building runs a residents’ evening every year, the safest approach is to fix next December’s date as soon as this one is over. Standard prices apply throughout December, with a premium only on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.

## For charities A choir that can fill a hired church and still sit quietly through the appeal

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

### How we work with charity event teams

You send the date, the church, the expected attendance, and the rough shape of the evening. We come back within 48 hours with a written quote, a recommended number of singers, and a draft running order you can put in front of a committee. Most charity carol concerts land at a full choir of eight singers (from £2,000) or a twelve-voice chorus (from £3,000) where the church is large and the ticket allocation is ambitious. A small choir of four (from £1,150) does the job in a chapel or a smaller parish church. Every figure sits on the pricing page , and none of them change in December.

A carol concert asks two different things of a choir on the same night. For the congregational carols the singers lead from the front and hold the line against several hundred people, most of whom know the first verse well and the third verse not at all. For the choir-only items they perform to an audience that has stopped singing and is listening. We rehearse both, and we programme them so the evening alternates rather than front-loading one and then the other.

Accompaniment depends on the building. Where the church has a working organ we bring an organist (from £250), which is what congregational singing wants underneath it. Where there is no organ, or no one available to play it, the choir sings the whole concert a cappella and still leads the carols. If your evening has mulled wine or a reception either side of the music, there is a package with background piano between the choir’s sets.

On timing: our December church dates go by mid‑September, and the churches themselves are usually booked before that. Charities tend to fix the venue first, which is sensible. Send us the date the moment the church confirms it.


### What your audience and donors receive

Carols they already know, sung well enough that they sing louder. The repertoire covers all the traditional carols, with descants where a big last verse is wanted, and we arrange popular Christmas songs a cappella for the points in the programme that want something lighter than a hymn. If your cause suggests a particular piece, we will arrange it for the ensemble you have booked.

The choir works to your running order rather than its own. When a patron or celebrity reader is at the lectern the singers are seated and still, with no shuffling of copies while someone speaks. The appeal is the moment that most often gets mishandled: you can have quiet singing underneath it, or silence and the collection plates. Decide at the planning stage and it goes on the running sheet with everything else.

Dress is concert black unless you ask for something else. The choir arrives an hour before doors open, walks the building with the organist, and rehearses the joins — the second where a reading finishes and the next carol has to start. That is the thing that falls apart in an under-rehearsed concert, and it is what your audience notices.

Summary: Abide With Me is the most-requested funeral hymn in the UK. Read why families choose it, hear it sung by The London Choral Service, and find the full text.

## Abide With Me — the most-requested funeral hymn

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 2 May 2026

Abide With Me is the most-commonly-chosen closing hymn at British funerals — alongside The Lord’s My Shepherd, which is the most widely known, the two are the most-requested funeral hymns in the UK. Families request it whether the person who died was religious or not, whether the service is in a Norman parish church or a 1970s crematorium chapel, and whether the congregation numbers fifteen or three hundred. The hymn has held its place in British funeral life for more than a century.


### The words were written by a dying man

Henry Francis Lyte wrote Abide With Me in 1847, in his last weeks of life. He was a curate in the fishing port of Brixham, Devon, and tuberculosis was killing him. He preached his final sermon on a Sunday in September, walked back to the rectory, and finished the hymn that evening. He died that November in the south of France, where he had gone in a last attempt at recovery.

You can hear this in every line. “Swift to its close ebbs out life’s little day; earth’s joys grow dim, its glories pass away.” A man who knew he was dying wrote those words. They carry the weight of a person staring at the same thing the bereaved congregation is now facing. That is why they land so hard. Lyte is not consoling from a safe distance; he is writing from inside the same fear.

The famous closing line — “In life, in death, O Lord, abide with me” — is not a request for relief. It is a request for company. Stay close. Don’t leave. That is what we want at a funeral, on either side of the coffin, and the hymn says so plainly.


### The melody is built for grief

The tune, Eventide, was written by William Henry Monk in 1861. The story goes that he composed it in ten minutes one evening after his daughter died, watching the sun set with his wife. Whether or not the story is exactly true, the music sounds like it. There is a stillness in the melodic line that nothing else in the hymn repertoire quite achieves.

What makes Eventide work at a funeral is its restraint. It never asks the congregation to reach for a high note in a moment of vulnerability. The melody sits comfortably in the middle of an average voice. It moves in steady, even quavers without dramatic intervals. People who have not sung a hymn in twenty years can find it within the first phrase. People who can barely speak through their tears can still mouth the words and stay with the rest of the room.

The harmonic progression is gentle too — mostly conventional, but with one moment of real beauty in each verse, where the underlying chord shifts under the word that matters most. In verse four, that moment lands on “ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness.” In verse five, it lands on “Heaven’s morning breaks.” A skilled organist or choir can lean into these moments without anyone noticing the technique, and the congregation steadies.


### It works in any setting

We have sung Abide With Me at Westminster Abbey for a memorial service of three hundred and fifty mourners, and at a crematorium in Mortlake for a private family of nine. It works equally well in both. The hymn does not need a grand acoustic to do its job. A solo singer with no accompaniment in a chapel of rest can still bring the whole room to silence with the first verse.

For Anglican and Free Church funerals it sits in the standard tradition. For Catholic services it works as a non-liturgical hymn outside the Mass — usually after the eulogy or as the coffin is brought in. For non-religious or humanist services, families often choose it anyway, because the words speak more about presence and love than about doctrine. We rarely suggest replacing it with something less religious; if it is what the family wants, it usually fits.

Outside of funerals, Abide With Me is associated with the FA Cup Final, where it has been sung at Wembley since 1927. That association does not weaken the hymn at funerals; if anything, it deepens it. Many men in particular find it the one hymn they know, the one they have sung shoulder to shoulder with strangers, and the one that comes back to them when they have to sing it for someone they have loved.


### What it sounds like with a choir

A congregation singing Abide With Me with only an organ is moving. A congregation singing Abide With Me with a professional choir leading them is something else entirely. The choir holds the line when voices in the pews falter, lifts the sound when the organ alone could not, and adds harmonic depth that makes the hymn feel as substantial as it is.

We typically arrange Abide With Me to build through its verses. Verse one in unison: just the melody, supported quietly by the organ. Verse two in two parts. Verse three opens to four-part harmony. By verse five the choir is in full voice and the congregation has been carried up with them, often singing more confidently than they thought they could. The final “In life, in death” lands with the kind of weight only live music produces in a sacred space.

A recording of our choir singing Abide With Me. Hear more recordings .


### Where to place it in the service

Abide With Me works best as the closing hymn of a funeral. The text is explicitly about facing the end of life with company and grace, and that is the note many families want to leave the service on. Sung last, with the choir in full voice and the congregation carried with them, it sends people out into the rest of the day with something solid to hold.

If the family wants two or three hymns, Abide With Me sits well in second or third position. We often suggest opening with something more pastoral — The Lord’s My Shepherd, for instance, or All Things Bright and Beautiful for someone who loved the natural world — and then placing Abide With Me later in the service when the congregation has settled and is ready for its weight.

It also pairs naturally with non-hymn pieces. After Schubert’s Ave Maria sung by a soloist, Abide With Me as the closing congregational hymn brings everyone back into the room together. After a Bach chorale or a piece of Fauré, it grounds the service in something familiar after something unfamiliar. For more ideas on structuring funeral music, see our complete guide to choosing funeral music or our list of popular funeral hymns .


### What families tell us

People remember the moment Abide With Me starts. They remember the silence in the room before the organ comes in. They remember the first time the whole congregation joined the choir on the second verse. They remember standing afterwards, surprised at how much steadier they felt than they had at the start of the service. We hear this from families months later, sometimes years later.

Choosing funeral music can feel overwhelming, especially when you are already dealing with so much. If you would like to talk through whether Abide With Me is right for the service, or how it might fit alongside other pieces, please get in touch. There is no charge for the conversation and no obligation at all.

Summary: Jerusalem by Hubert Parry is one of the most thrilling wedding hymns ever written. Full text, history, and a live recording by The London Choral Service.

## Jerusalem — the most British of wedding hymns

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 2 May 2026

No other hymn in the English repertoire opens a wedding ceremony quite like Jerusalem. The first chord lands like a stage cue. The congregation knows what is coming. By the second line, even the people who haven’t sung in years are singing.


### Where the hymn comes from

The text is by William Blake, written around 1804 as the preface to a longer poem called Milton. The poem itself is dense and visionary, but the preface stands alone: four short verses asking whether Christ once walked “upon England’s mountains green”, and ending with the famous demand to bring me my bow of burning gold and build a new Jerusalem “in England’s green and pleasant land”.

Hubert Parry set it to music in 1916 at the request of Robert Bridges, then Poet Laureate, who wanted a song to lift the spirits of a country exhausted by war. Parry composed it in a single sitting and Bridges arranged for it to be sung at a Fight for Right meeting at the Queen’s Hall on 28 March 1916. It was an immediate success. Within two years it was the unofficial anthem of the women’s suffrage movement, and within five it had become a fixture of British public life.

The hymn took a few decades to settle into wedding repertoire, but by the second half of the twentieth century it was firmly there. The 2011 wedding of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge used it as a congregational hymn at Westminster Abbey. Many couples now choose it because their parents and grandparents sang it at the same point in their own services.


### What makes the music work

Parry’s setting is short, simple, and structurally bold. The melody starts low, rises through the first two phrases, and then opens out into a soaring third phrase that takes most of the congregation by surprise the first time they sing it. The pattern repeats for the second verse, and on the second time around even reluctant singers are with you.

The harmonies are conventional but used with extraordinary skill. There is one moment in particular — the sustained chord under “O clouds, unfold!” in verse two — where the music holds the congregation in suspension before resolving into the final phrase. A good organist will lean into that suspension, and the congregation leans with them.

The orchestration most often heard at weddings was made by Edward Elgar in 1922, who scored Parry’s organ part for full orchestra at the request of George V. The Elgar version is what you hear at the Last Night of the Proms. For most weddings, a strong organ is enough. But if the venue has the resources for trumpets or a brass ensemble, Jerusalem with brass adds a layer of grandeur that few other pieces in the repertoire can match.


### It suits more weddings than you might think

The obvious associations — royal weddings, the Last Night of the Proms, England rugby internationals — can make couples worry that Jerusalem will feel too grand or too patriotic for their ceremony. In practice, it almost never does.

For a large wedding in a substantial church or cathedral, Jerusalem is the natural opening hymn. It establishes the scale of the occasion, settles the congregation, and gives the choir something to lean into from the first bar. For a smaller wedding in a parish church, it works just as well as a closing hymn — sending guests out into the rest of the day with their spirits lifted.

The text is religious enough to suit a Church of England wedding without being so doctrinal that it excludes guests of other faiths or no faith. Blake’s vision is more about hope and possibility than about specific theology, and that suits a wedding well. Many couples choose it precisely because it speaks to what marriage is really about: the work of building something good, together, in the world you have.

Jerusalem is also a strong choice for memorial services, civic occasions, and corporate carol concerts that include a non-Christmas piece. Its breadth of association means it can find a home in almost any kind of formal gathering.


### What it sounds like with a choir

Parry wrote Jerusalem for unison voices over a strong organ, and that is how it usually sounds in church. A congregation singing it well, with the organ supporting them, is one of the great experiences of British public worship.

With a professional choir leading the congregation, the hymn becomes something more. The choir can take the first verse in unison alongside the congregation, then split into harmony for the second verse, lifting the sound and giving the climactic phrases the weight they deserve. The descant on the final “in England’s green and pleasant land” — sung high above the melody by the sopranos — turns the final verse into something the congregation will talk about at the reception.

For larger weddings, we often arrange Jerusalem for choir with optional brass and trumpet fanfare into the introduction. A short trumpet voluntary before the organ comes in, the choir laying the harmony underneath the congregation in verse one, the descant lifting in verse two: it is the kind of arrangement that makes a wedding feel like an event of national consequence even if there are only seventy people in the room. You can hear our singers perform a range of wedding hymns on our listening page.


### Where to place it in the service

Jerusalem works best as the opening hymn or the closing hymn. As an opener, it announces the wedding with confidence. As a closer, it sends the congregation out on a high. It works less well in the middle of a service: its energy is too big to settle a congregation back into reflection after a reading or sermon.

If you are having two hymns and Jerusalem is one of them, pair it with something gentler. Be Thou My Vision is a natural counterweight — quieter, more intimate, and beautifully placed after the readings if Jerusalem opens the service. Love Divine, All Loves Excelling sits well too. Avoid pairing Jerusalem with another large hymn like Guide Me, O Thou Great Redeemer; the service will feel front-loaded with sound.

For three hymns, an order of Jerusalem (opening) — Be Thou My Vision (middle, after the readings) — All Things Bright and Beautiful or Praise My Soul, the King of Heaven (closing) gives a lovely arc: large, intimate, joyful. For more on structuring wedding music, see our guide to choosing wedding hymns or our walkthrough of wedding ceremony music .


### What couples tell us

The thing couples mention most often after a wedding that opened with Jerusalem is the moment they walked down the aisle to it. The hymn was not chosen as the processional — it came after — but the energy in the room from singing it together as the first thing the congregation did set the tone for the whole service. Several have told us the photograph of the choir hitting the descant on the final verse, with the bride and groom turning to look back at the congregation, is the photo from the day they keep on the wall.


### We’re here if you’d like a hand

If Jerusalem is on your list, or if you would like to talk through whether it suits your venue and the rest of your music, please get in touch. We can advise on whether to add brass, where to place the descant, how to pair it with other hymns, and what arrangement will work best in your particular church. There is no charge for the conversation and no obligation.

You might also find these guides helpful: our guide to choosing wedding hymns covers the most popular options, wedding ceremony music walks through every musical moment from processional to recessional, and our guide to Be Thou My Vision covers the hymn most often paired with Jerusalem at weddings.

Summary: Why Marco Frisina's Anima Christi suits a Catholic wedding Mass, where the Latin prayer sits in the liturgy, and what it sounds like sung by our choir.

## Anima Christi at a Catholic wedding

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 15 August 2026

Anima Christi is a prayer about not being parted from the one you love. Couples planning a Nuptial Mass meet it at the Communion, the one stretch of the liturgy where the parish has ruled out anything secular and Ave Maria is already spoken for. Marco Frisina’s setting of the Latin is the version we are asked for most.

Our quintet singing Frisina’s Anima Christi. Hear more recordings .


### The prayer is older than its reputation

Anima Christi appears in manuscripts from around 1300, two centuries before St Ignatius of Loyola put it at the front of the Spiritual Exercises. Most people still credit Ignatius with writing it. He recognised a good prayer and handed it to his order, and the Jesuits carried it across the Catholic world.

You move through a run of short petitions — sanctify me, save me, wash me, strengthen me, hear me — and then reach the line couples notice: Ne permittas me separari a te . Never let me be parted from you. The prayer addresses Christ. Sung twenty minutes after you have made a promise in almost those words, in front of everyone you know, it also sounds like a line about your marriage.


### Frisina’s setting

Monsignor Marco Frisina is a priest of the Diocese of Rome. He founded the diocesan choir that sings at the great liturgies in the city and ran the Vicariate’s office for sacred music for years, alongside writing scores for Italian television’s biblical films. English-speaking parishes sing his Anima Christi more than anything else he wrote.

He keeps the Latin and gives it a long, unhurried melody that sits in a comfortable part of the voice, so no singer has to reach for it. The harmony underneath is plain. He wrote the piece for parish forces, which is why it holds up with one voice and an organ, and why adding singers deepens it instead of making it louder.


### Where it goes in a Nuptial Mass

It goes at the Communion. Anima Christi is one of the prayers of thanksgiving after Mass printed in the Roman Missal, so at a wedding Mass it belongs during the distribution or straight after. That is also the longest unscripted gap in the service, and the one your organist fills with an improvisation when nobody has chosen anything for it.

If you are also laying flowers at the Lady altar, keep Ave Maria for that and let Anima Christi cover the Communion. The two moments sit about five minutes apart and do different jobs: one is a devotion to Our Lady, the other is the whole church praying after receiving.

For a wedding outside Mass, which is usual when one of you is not Catholic, there is no Communion. The piece then works during the signing of the register, where you need three or four minutes of music and the congregation has nothing to do. Our guide to wedding ceremony music sets out the full running order, and choosing wedding hymns covers what the congregation sings.


### Why the parish will say yes

Parishes vary in how much they police wedding music, and some dioceses ask to approve the list in advance. A Latin liturgical text set by a serving Roman priest clears that test. No parish has yet queried it with us.

Couples reach us three weeks out, after a priest has turned down a film theme or a pop ballad, needing a replacement the parish will not refuse as well. Anima Christi answers that without feeling like second best, which is why we suggest it when a couple is in that position.


### The line about death

Know one thing before you commit to it. Towards the end the text asks in hora mortis meae voca me — in the hour of my death, call me — and then, bid me come to you.

Some couples hear the strongest available reading of the promise they have made, the thought behind “till death do us part” turned around and pointed at God. Others would rather nothing at their wedding mentioned death. Both reactions are reasonable, and we would rather you decided now than found out from the order of service.


### Who sings it, and what it costs

Anima Christi can be sung as a hymn, and some parishes sing it that way at Sunday Mass. At a wedding it is normally the choir or a soloist, with the congregation listening through the Communion rather than joining in.

Three sets of forces work. A soloist with an organist starts from £450 and carries the melody alone, which suits a small church or a short Mass. Four singers add harmony from £1,150 and cover your hymns and responses as well. The quintet in the recording above starts from £1,400: the second soprano frees one voice for the melody while the other four support it, and that is the version most couples pick once they have heard it. The full table is on our pricing page .

We bring our own copies, rehearse in the church before your guests arrive, and speak to your parish organist or director of music beforehand so that nobody is improvising on the day. If you want the piece in English, or transposed for a particular singer, say so early and we will have it written.

The companion to this article is our guide to Anima Christi at a Catholic funeral , which covers the same piece in the other service families ask for it at.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Is Anima Christi allowed at a Catholic wedding?

Yes. The text is a Latin prayer of the Roman rite, printed in the Missal among the prayers of thanksgiving after Mass, and Marco Frisina is a priest of the Diocese of Rome. Parishes that refuse secular music accept it without discussion. Send your priest the full music list anyway, because some dioceses ask to see it in advance.


#### Where does Anima Christi go in a Catholic wedding?

During Communion, or immediately after it. Anima Christi is a prayer of thanksgiving after Communion, so that is where it belongs in a Nuptial Mass. At a wedding outside Mass there is no Communion, and the piece works during the signing of the register instead.


#### Does the congregation sing Anima Christi, or the choir?

The choir or a soloist. It can be sung as a hymn, and some parishes do, but at a Catholic wedding the congregation normally listens to it through the Communion. A soloist with an organist starts from £450, a quartet from £1,150, and the quintet in the recording on this page from £1,400.

## Anima Christi at a Catholic funeral

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 15 August 2026

Anima Christi asks Christ for one thing at the end: in hora mortis meae voca me — in the hour of my death, call me. Families planning a Requiem Mass arrive at the piece through that line. Marco Frisina’s setting gives the Latin a melody a congregation can follow the first time it hears it.

Our quintet singing Frisina’s Anima Christi. Hear more recordings .


### A prayer from about 1300

The text is anonymous and turns up in manuscripts from the early fourteenth century. St Ignatius of Loyola placed it at the opening of the Spiritual Exercises two hundred years later, which is why so many people credit him with writing it. For families with a Jesuit connection — a school, a parish, a brother in the Society — that association is part of why they ask for it.

The prayer moves through short petitions and then turns, in its last lines, towards death: hide me within your wounds, never let me be parted from you, call me in the hour of my death, bid me come to you. You do not have to explain any of that to a congregation at a funeral. Print the English beside the Latin and the room follows it.


### Your parents may know it as Soul of My Saviour

Soul of My Saviour is a metrical English translation of the same prayer, sung to William Maher’s tune Anima Christi. Most Catholics schooled in Britain before the 1980s know it by heart. Older mourners will recognise the words in Frisina’s setting without recognising the music, which at a funeral is often the right combination: familiar enough to hold on to, unfamiliar enough that it does not belong to somebody else’s service.

If the congregation is elderly and you would rather they sang, use Soul of My Saviour as a hymn and keep Frisina’s setting for a moment when the singers are on their own. Our guide to hymns for a Catholic funeral covers the rest of the repertoire and where each piece falls in the Mass.


### Frisina’s setting

Monsignor Marco Frisina is a priest of the Diocese of Rome who founded the diocesan choir and ran the Vicariate’s office for sacred music. His Anima Christi keeps the Latin and sets it to a long melodic line over plain harmony, sitting in a comfortable part of the voice. He wrote it for parish forces rather than cathedral ones, so it holds up with a single singer and an organ.

At a funeral that keeps the piece from becoming a performance. No singer has to brace for a high note, and nobody in the pews stops following the prayer to watch a soloist work. The music stays quiet and keeps moving.


### Where it goes in a Requiem Mass

The Communion is the natural place. Anima Christi is a thanksgiving after Communion, and the distribution at a Requiem runs long enough to carry a piece of this length without the music running out or overstaying.

It also works at the Final Commendation, sung while the priest incenses the coffin. The text asks to be called, and the liturgy asks the same thing at the same moment. It suits the vigil the evening before, and the reception of the body into church.

It does not work as the recessional. The prayer is inward and quiet, and a coffin leaving a church wants something the congregation can stand up and sing: Abide With Me or How Great Thou Art will do more there. Our complete funeral music guide walks through the whole service in order.


### Who sings it, and what it costs

Anima Christi can be sung as a hymn, and some parishes sing it that way at Sunday Mass. At a funeral it is normally the choir or a soloist, with the congregation listening. That is worth having at a funeral: the hymn a family dreads is usually the one they cannot finish, and this asks nothing of them.

A soloist with an organist starts from £450, which is what most families book for a crematorium chapel or a small parish church. Four singers, from £1,150, give you harmony on this and cover the hymns as well. The recording above is a quintet, from £1,400: the second soprano frees one voice for the melody while the other four support it. Prices are on our pricing page , and for a funeral at short notice we can usually confirm availability the same day.

The Latin needs no rehearsal from anyone but us. We bring copies, arrive an hour early, and settle the running order with the priest and the funeral director before the family arrives.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What does Anima Christi mean?

Soul of Christ. The Latin prayer opens Anima Christi, sanctifica me — Soul of Christ, sanctify me — and runs through a sequence of petitions to its closing request: in the hour of my death, call me, and bid me come to you. The English hymn Soul of My Saviour is a metrical translation of the same text.


#### Is Anima Christi suitable for a Catholic funeral Mass?

Yes. It is a prayer of thanksgiving after Communion from the Roman rite, so it sits naturally at the Communion of a Requiem Mass, and it also works at the Final Commendation. Parishes that restrict secular music at funerals accept it without question.


#### Does the congregation sing Anima Christi at a funeral?

Normally not. It can be sung as a hymn, and some parishes do, but at a Catholic funeral it is usually the choir or a soloist while the congregation listens. A soloist with an organist starts from £450, a quartet from £1,150, and the quintet in the recording on this page from £1,400.


#### Should the order of service print the Latin?

We would print the Latin with an English translation beside it. It lets the congregation follow the prayer while the choir sings, and it gives people something to hold at a point in the service where there is nothing else to do.

If you would like to talk through whether Anima Christi belongs in the service, or how it sits alongside the hymns the parish has suggested, please get in touch. There is no charge for the conversation and no obligation. Most funeral bookings reach us at short notice and we are used to working to a few days.
