Summary: How live carol singers work in a hotel: lobby sets, festive afternoon tea, ballroom singalongs, what they cost, and why December fills by mid-September.

## Christmas entertainment for hotels

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

A hotel at Christmas has something almost no other venue has: a building already full of people. Guests come down for afternoon tea, drop bags at the desk, wait for a table, stand about with a glass before dinner. Live carol singers turn those in-between minutes into the part of the stay guests film and put online. And they ask very little of the building — no stage, no power, no sound check. This guide covers which format suits a lobby, a tea room, and a ballroom, how to schedule singers across December, what the choir wears and sings, and what to settle before you sign.


### Why live carol singers work in a hotel

Most festive budgets go on things guests look at: the tree in the atrium, the garlands up the staircase, the window display. Live singing is the only part of that spend guests stop for. Four voices starting Silent Night in a marble lobby empty the lift queue and refill it thirty seconds later with people holding phones up. Those clips go onto guest accounts with your hotel tagged, which is a return the garlands do not produce.

The practical case is shorter. A professional choir singing a cappella needs a patch of floor and somewhere to leave coats. Nothing gets plugged in, no cable crosses a guest route, no engineer has to be booked, and there is no sound check to schedule around lunch service. Trained voices carry across a lobby or a restaurant on their own; that is what the training is for. If your lounge has a piano and you want it used, we can send a pianist too, though the singing does not depend on one.

One thing does need checking: the room itself. Hard surfaces flatter unaccompanied voices, so a stone stair, a glass atrium, or the back wall of a bar all help the sound reach the far end. A low lounge with deep carpet and a full sitting in progress absorbs a great deal, and there you want six voices rather than four, or the singers moved to where the ceiling is highest. Describe the space when you enquire and we will tell you the number.


### Formats by space

The same singers can work four quite different rooms in a hotel, and the format changes with each one.


#### The lobby

Two approaches. Roaming means the group moves through the space in a loose knot, sings three or four carols in one spot, then relocates — by the tree, at the foot of the stairs, near the concierge desk. That suits the arrivals peak, when the audience changes every few minutes and nobody stays long enough for a full set. Stationary means the singers hold one position and the room comes to them, which suits the drinks hour once people have settled. Plenty of hotels use both inside one booking: roaming from four o’clock, stationary once the bar fills.


#### Festive afternoon tea

Afternoon tea wants background singing, and background singing wants gaps. Twenty minutes on, twenty minutes off, repeated across the sitting, lets tables talk between sets and gives every seating in the room something rather than loading it all onto the first hour. Where the tea room has a piano, the usual booking is choir with background piano between sets: the pianist covers the gaps so the room is never silent and the singers still get their breaks. Where there is no piano, we can bring a keyboard and speaker. That carries an extra charge, and it appears in the written quote before you commit.


#### Restaurant and ballroom

A private dining room or a ballroom party is a performance job rather than a background one. The singers stand as a group, the room turns to face them, and the set runs fifteen to twenty-five minutes: two or three unaccompanied carols, an arrangement of something the guests know from the radio, then a singalong finale on Hark! The Herald Angels Sing or O Come, All Ye Faithful . The singalong is what makes a corporate table of forty behave like a party rather than a dinner. Print the words on the menu card or hand out song sheets and you will get several times the voices.


#### Frontage, terraces, and light switch-ons

The choir can sing outdoors. A switch-on at the front door, carols on a terrace with mulled wine, singers on the steps as a coach party arrives — all workable, and unamplified voices hold up in open air when the crowd is gathered round rather than spread across a square. Cold is the limiting factor rather than the acoustic: the singers need somewhere warm to wait, and outdoor sets run shorter for that reason. For a switch-on, send us the countdown time so the carol lands on the moment the lights come up.


### Scheduling across the season

Two shapes of booking cover most hotels. A one-off evening — the staff party, a residents’ drinks, the switch-on — is a single date with a single agreed format. A recurring booking puts the same singers in the building on several December dates: every Saturday of festive afternoon tea, say, or the three Fridays before Christmas. The recurring version is worth raising early. It fixes the dates in one conversation, and it gives you the same faces each time, which matters once your duty manager has briefed them on where to stand and when to stop for the speeches.

A standard Christmas booking is up to an hour and a half of the choir’s time, including their breaks. Inside that you can have one long set or three short ones, and the shape is yours to choose. Programmes that run longer are perfectly possible; they carry a premium, quoted upfront in writing rather than added to the invoice afterwards. If you are hiring the choir into a church service instead, the booking is measured by the length of the service.


### What the singers wear

Dress should follow the room rather than the season, and you choose it. Concert dress — long black, black tie — suits a ballroom, a gala dinner, or a formal afternoon tea. All black without the formality suits a lobby set that should read as part of the building. Casual suits a family switch-on or a market. Christmas jumpers are available if the evening wants them, and we carry Santa hats to go with any of the above. Period costume is the one thing we do not offer. Tell us what your own front-of-house team is wearing that night and we will pitch it to match.


### Repertoire for a mixed guest list

The repertoire is the traditional carol book plus a cappella arrangements of the popular Christmas songs. On the carol side, the singers know O Come, All Ye Faithful , In the Bleak Midwinter , Silent Night , the Sussex Carol , and Ding Dong Merrily on High by heart. On the other side sit close-harmony versions of Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas , White Christmas , and Winter Wonderland .

That balance matters more in a hotel than almost anywhere else, because your guest list is not all British and not all churchgoing. A couple visiting from Tokyo for the shopping may never have heard Once in Royal David’s City ; they will recognise White Christmas within two bars. Tell us roughly who is in the building that week — a corporate block booking, half-term families, an international leisure mix — and we weight the running order accordingly. Sheet music, rehearsal, and the programme are handled at our end.

December fills from the top. Our December diary closes out by mid-September, and the Fridays and Saturdays of the second and third weeks go first. Read this in the summer and you are choosing your date; ring in November and you are choosing from what is left. A late enquiry is still worth making, because cancellations happen, but the range of ensemble sizes narrows quickly.

Live carol singers, in one of two shapes. Roaming: the group moves between the tree, the stairs, and the concierge desk across the arrivals peak. No. A professional choir sings a cappella, so the booking needs a patch of floor and somewhere to leave coats. There is no staging, no power, no speakers, no sound check. Yes, and hotels often book that way: the same singers on every Saturday of festive afternoon tea, or on the three Fridays before Christmas. Booking the dates together fixes them before the diary fills and means the group already knows your room and your timings. Ask early, because December closes out by mid-September.

Summary: Planning a residents' carol evening in a lobby or courtyard — the running order, song sheets, mulled wine, timings, and what a professional choir costs to hire.

## Hosting a residents’ carol event

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

A carol evening is the least complicated event a building runs all year. Nothing needs catering beyond mulled wine and a tray of mince pies, and because a professional choir sings unaccompanied there is no stage to build, no power to run, and no sound system to hire. A lobby will do. This guide is for property managers, estate teams, and residents’ association committees working out where to hold one, how to shape the evening, and what booking a choir for it costs.


### Why a carol evening works as a residents’ event

Most buildings try a summer party at some point, and most find it hard work. Catering, a licence, a wet-weather plan, and somebody standing over a barbecue for three hours. A carol evening asks far less of whoever organises it, and it pulls a wider spread of residents through the door. People who would never come to a drinks party will come down for half an hour if there is singing and something hot to hold.

It also gives neighbours a reason to speak to one another. A block of eighty flats can go a whole year with nobody learning a name beyond their own landing. Twenty minutes standing in a lobby with a paper cup while four singers work through Once in Royal David’s City does more for that than any number of newsletters.

For the managing agent or the committee, it is an easy thing to be seen doing. The spend is small against a service-charge budget, and you come away with the photographs that go in the January residents’ update.


### Choosing the space

You almost certainly already have the room. The choir sings a cappella, so nothing needs plugging in, nobody needs a platform, and the singers can either hold one position or move through the space as people arrive.

The lobby. The default, and usually the right answer. Hard floors and a high ceiling give unaccompanied voices a generous acoustic, which is the same reason carols sound good in a church. Singers can group near the lifts or the concierge desk, or work the room as residents come in from the street. If the entrance has to keep functioning as an entrance, tell us and the singers will position themselves out of the traffic.

The courtyard or podium garden. Outdoors is fine, and in December it often looks better: residents come down in coats, and whatever lighting the landscaping already has does the rest. Cold air does not trouble professional singers. Rain does, so agree an indoor fallback when you book rather than at five o’clock on the day.

The communal lounge or club room. The better choice for a building with older or less mobile residents, and better again where there is a piano in the corner. Soft furnishings absorb a great deal of sound, so a room like this suits four to six voices rather than a larger group.

Outside the front entrance. Singing on the steps or under a portico catches residents on their way home and is the most visible option from the street. Check the estate’s own rules first, and if the singers would be standing on public pavement, check with the local authority too.


### Shaping the evening

Residents’ carol evenings tend to settle into the same shape, and it is a good one. Drinks first, singing in sets, everybody joining in at the end.

- Mulled wine and mince pies from the start. A table by the door, someone pouring, and twenty minutes for people to arrive. Soft drinks matter more here than at a corporate party — half the room will be walking children back upstairs afterwards.
- Two or three sets of about twenty minutes. Sets beat continuous singing at a residents’ event, because the breaks are the part where the neighbours actually talk to each other. Three sets with two breaks fills ninety minutes comfortably.
- A singalong to finish. Print song sheets: four or five carols everyone half-knows, words only, one side of A4. Hark the Herald , O Come All Ye Faithful , Silent Night and Away in a Manger will get a lobby going. The choir leads the tune and holds the harmony underneath, so nobody has to be brave on their own.
If the building has a lot of families, run the singalong earlier and let the last set belong to whoever is still standing. Children lose interest at about the forty-minute mark. An evening that ends while the room still wants more is the one the committee gets asked to repeat.


### Piano between the sets

Where a building has a piano — an upright in the club room, a grand in the lounge — we can send a pianist alongside the choir and have them play quietly through the breaks so the room never falls silent. A pianist starts from £225 on top of the choir’s fee. Where there is no piano and you still want accompaniment, we can bring a keyboard and a speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in your written quote so nothing appears later on the invoice.

Neither is necessary. The choir is fully a cappella by default, and unaccompanied singing in a hard-floored lobby is the better sound in most buildings anyway.


### What the singers wear

Concert dress is the default. All black is a step down from that, ordinary casual clothes a step further, and for a building with a lot of children, Christmas jumpers usually land best. We have Santa hats if you want them. Tell us the tone you are after when you book and the singers will match it.


### Repertoire

The choir carries the whole traditional carol repertoire, from Once in Royal David’s City and In the Bleak Midwinter to The Sussex Carol and O Holy Night , alongside a cappella arrangements of the popular Christmas songs people actually hum in December. Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas sits perfectly well next to a fifteenth-century carol in a lobby, and in a residential building that mixture usually works better than either on its own.

Say at the booking stage whether you would rather the programme leaned secular or churchy. There is enough repertoire either way, and Luca builds the running order around what you tell him about the building.


### How long the choir sings for

A standard booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks, which covers the shape above with time in hand. Longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront in the written quote before you commit to anything. Ninety minutes is enough for almost every building. Attention in a lobby has a natural half-life, and the singing is there to draw people down rather than hold them captive.


### Budget, and how it looks per household

Our standard prices apply in December. There is no Christmas uplift, so a carol evening on the tenth of December costs what the same choir costs in June. The exceptions are Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, which carry a premium confirmed in the written quote. A Small Choir of four singers is from £1,150, a sextet from £1,600, and a full choir of eight from £2,000, inclusive of all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. Full detail is on our pricing page .

For a service-charge line or an association budget, the number that carries a meeting is the one per household. A Small Choir at £1,150 across a building of 60 flats is a little over £19 a flat; across 120 flats it is under £10. A sextet at £1,600 in that same 120-flat building comes to about £13 each. Set against the annual spend on planting or the lobby Christmas tree, a carol evening is rarely the line anyone argues about.

Where the money comes from is your call. Some buildings run it through the community-events line in the service charge, some through a residents’ association float, and some through a marketing budget where units are still being let or sold. Whichever route you take, the fee is for the evening rather than a charge per resident, so a larger building gets the better arithmetic.


### Book by early autumn

December dates go by the middle of September most years, and the first three weeks of the month are the tightest in the choral calendar. Residents’ events have one advantage over corporate ones: a Tuesday or Wednesday evening in early December is far easier to fill than a Friday, and it is the same choir either way. If your committee or your client meets quarterly, put the carol evening on the summer agenda rather than the autumn one.

The London Choral Service sings at residents’ evenings across London and the rest of the UK. For how we work with managing agents and estate teams, see our information for property managers ; for ensemble sizes and the formats the singers work in, see hire carol singers .


### Frequently asked questions


#### What happens at a residents’ carol evening?

Residents come down to the lobby or the courtyard for mulled wine and mince pies, the choir sings two or three sets of carols with breaks between them, and the evening finishes with a singalong from printed song sheets. Ninety minutes covers the whole thing. The singers are unaccompanied, so nothing needs setting up beyond a table for the drinks.


#### Can carol singers perform in an apartment lobby or courtyard?

Yes, and both suit the music. A lobby’s hard floors and high ceiling flatter unaccompanied voices, and a courtyard works well in December provided you agree an indoor fallback in case of rain. The choir sings a cappella, so no power supply, stage, or sound system is needed. The singers can hold one position or move through the space as residents arrive.


#### How much does a residents’ carol event cost?

A Small Choir of four singers is from £1,150, a sextet from £1,600, and a full choir of eight from £2,000, inclusive of all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. We charge no Christmas uplift, so a December date costs what any other date costs. Across a building of 60 flats, a Small Choir works out at a little over £19 a household.


#### Do residents sing along, or just listen?

Both, and the evening is better for having both. The choir’s own sets are there to be listened to, with arrangements that four or six trained voices can handle and a crowd cannot. The singalong at the end belongs to everyone: print word sheets for four or five well-known carols, and the choir leads the tune while holding the harmony underneath.

## When to book Christmas entertainment

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

A choir can only be in one place on a given evening. That one fact governs everything else about booking live music for Christmas. From the last week of November onwards, offices, hotels, livery halls, and charities all want the same few evenings, and the diary fills in the order the enquiries arrive. This guide explains how December works from the performer’s side of the desk: which dates disappear first, what is realistically still available in October and November, and what The London Choral Service needs from you to hold a date.


### How December works for live performers

The pressure in December is not spread evenly across the month. It concentrates on the first three weeks; within those weeks on Thursday and Friday; and within those days on the early evening, when guests arrive and the drinks go round. A choir of eight can sing one of those slots. If two clients want the same Thursday at six, one of them moves to another date, another time, or another ensemble.

There is a limit to how many ensembles we can field on the same evening. The singers we work with are professionals with their own December commitments in cathedrals, concert halls, and recording studios, and this is their busiest month too. When we tell you a date has gone, it means the singers for it are committed elsewhere.

The rest of the year this is a much easier conversation. A wedding in June or a corporate dinner in March can usually be covered at a few weeks’ notice, at any size. December is the one month where the date decides what is possible.


### The date that matters: mid-September

Most years the first three weeks of December are closed out by the middle of September. That is the pattern in our own diary, and it is the same figure we give event managers when they ask about lead times — see our information for event managers for how that sits alongside the rest of the year.

Enquiries that land in late September and October are mostly about the third week of December, midweek dates, and afternoons, because that is what remains. Enquiries in November are usually about ensemble size rather than date: whether four singers can do what twelve were wanted for. None of that means a late enquiry is wasted. It means the question changes from which date would you like? to what can still be assembled for this one?


### Month by month


#### Summer to early September

Everything is open. You choose the date first and the format second, which is the right way round. A Small Choir of four, a sextet, a full choir of eight, and a chorus of twelve are all available for the same evening at this stage, unaccompanied or with an organist. If your event has a fixed date — a board dinner, a carol service in a church you have already booked — this is the moment to lock it in.


#### Late September to October

Midweek availability is usually good. Prime Friday evenings in the first fortnight thin out fast, and by mid-October most of them have gone. Ensemble size becomes a constraint before the date does: we may have four singers free on a Friday when twelve are not. If your event can sit on a Tuesday or Wednesday, October is still a comfortable month to book.


#### November

Now we are working around bookings already in the diary. Smaller ensembles stay possible longer than large ones, for the obvious reason that four singers are easier to assemble than twelve. Off-peak days, afternoons, and the week running up to Christmas hold up best. Send us the date anyway. We would rather tell you within the day that it has gone than have you assume it has.


#### December itself

Occasionally possible, for off-peak days and times. For funerals we take short-notice work as a matter of course, because singers hold diary space open for exactly that. December has no such space, so we make no equivalent promise about Christmas. If your date is a Monday afternoon, or falls after the 20th, it is worth asking — send it over and we will confirm availability the same day.


### Christmas Eve and Christmas Day

We sing on both, including carols by candlelight on the 24th. Those two dates carry a premium, typically around 25 per cent, confirmed in the written quote before you commit to anything. They are also the first dates to go each year, ahead of everything in the first fortnight of December. If you want either one, ask well before September.


### What booking early gets you

Booking in the summer buys choice, not a lower price. Three things in particular:

- The ensemble you wanted. A chorus of twelve for a church that seats four hundred, or a Small Choir of four that can move through a lobby without blocking it. In September you pick; in November you take what is free.
- The time slot you wanted. Six o’clock on a Thursday in the first fortnight is the most requested hour of our year. In August it is still free.
- Time to plan the programme. Luca finalises the repertoire and coordinates arrival, positioning, and technical requirements with your venue. Booked in September, that work has weeks rather than days: readings placed between the carols, a piece for a soloist, a descant on the last verse of O Come, All Ye Faithful , a rehearsal with your chosen readers if the running order is complicated.
Late bookings still get a proper programme. They get it faster, with fewer options on the table, and with less room to accommodate a request that arrives the week before.


### What we need to confirm a date

Three details are enough to check availability: the date, the venue, and a rough sense of the format — carol service, drinks reception, office party, or a set during dinner. Headcount and a preferred ensemble size help, but they are not needed to start.

Send those and we come back with a proposal within 48 hours: ensemble options, a programme outline, and a written quote. If your date is tight, say so in the first email and we will check that date before anything else. If you would rather talk it through, call 07356 042468 .


### Prices do not rise at Christmas

There is no seasonal uplift. A Small Choir of four is £1,150 in December as in June, a sextet £1,600, a full choir of eight £2,000, and a chorus of twelve £3,000, inclusive of all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. An organist or pianist starts at £250. A standard Christmas booking runs up to 1.5 hours including breaks, or the length of a church service; longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront. The two exceptions to the standard rates are Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. Full figures are on our pricing page .

Waiting therefore costs you dates and ensemble sizes rather than money, which is a different kind of pressure from the one most seasonal booking advice describes.


### Frequently asked questions


#### When should you book Christmas party entertainment?

For a December date, book by early September. The London Choral Service closes out the first three weeks of December by the middle of September most years, and Thursday and Friday evenings in the first fortnight go before anything else. Booking over the summer gives you the widest choice of dates and ensemble sizes.


#### Is it too late to book carol singers in November or December?

Often not, and it is worth asking. By November we are working around bookings already in the diary, so a Small Choir of four or a midweek date is more likely to be free than a full choir on a Friday. In December itself we can sometimes cover an off-peak day, an afternoon, or a date after the 20th.


#### Is it cheaper to book Christmas entertainment early?

No. Our prices are the same in December as in June, with no seasonal uplift, and we do not discount for booking early. A Small Choir of four is £1,150 and a chorus of twelve £3,000, inclusive of all taxes, fees, and travel within Greater London. Booking early buys choice of date and ensemble size rather than a lower fee. Christmas Eve and Christmas Day are the exception: those two dates carry a premium, typically around 25 per cent, confirmed in the written quote.


#### Which December dates get booked first?

Christmas Eve and Christmas Day go first, then Thursday and Friday early evenings in the first two full weeks of December. Early-evening slots on other weekdays in that window follow. Afternoons, Mondays, and the days after the 20th hold up longest, so flexibility about the time of day widens your options more than flexibility about the week.

Summary: Booking carol singers through an agency or direct with a choir: how each route works, what a listing cannot tell you, and the questions to ask either way.

## Booking carol singers: agency or direct?

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

There are two ways to get carol singers into your December. You can go through an entertainment agency or a booking marketplace, which lists many acts and lets you compare them in one place. Or you can go direct to a choir that runs its own diary and deal with the musicians who will sing. Both routes get singers through the door. They differ in what you can find out before you commit, and in how much of the price you can see. This guide covers how each one works, and what to ask whichever you choose.


### How the carol-singing market is organised

Search for carol singers in October and most of what comes back belongs to entertainment agencies and booking marketplaces. These are platforms rather than performers. They carry profiles for hundreds of acts — jazz trios, string quartets, function bands, carol groups — and take your enquiry on behalf of whichever ones are free on your date and inside your budget. The act you end up booking is an independent supplier listed on the platform, and the platform handles the introduction, the contract, and usually the payment.

Alongside the platforms sit choirs and ensembles that take their own bookings. The London Choral Service is one of these. So are chamber choirs, professional consorts, and groups built around a fixed roster of singers under a named director. They are harder to find in one search, because nothing aggregates them onto a single page and they tend to rank for their own name rather than for “carol singers for hire”.

Neither structure is better in the abstract. They suit different jobs, and the sensible question is which one suits yours.


### What the agency route gives you

One enquiry, many acts. You describe the date, the venue, and the budget once, and hear back from several groups. For a first-time booker with no idea what a carol quartet costs, that is a fast way to calibrate.

Like-for-like comparison. Profiles on a platform follow the same template, so you can line up ensemble sizes, set lengths, and headline fees against each other without translating five different quote formats.

A familiar way to pay. Marketplaces carry messaging threads, standard contracts, card payment, and a review history for each act. If your finance team prefers a supplier with a payment platform behind it, that matters.

Bundling. If your party needs a choir, a DJ, and a photographer, doing all three through one platform saves you two conversations and one set of paperwork.


### What a listing cannot tell you

A profile page is a shop window for a group, and there are three things it will rarely answer without you asking.

Which singers arrive on the night. The photograph shows four people. The four who turn up on the eleventh of December may not be those four, because December is the busiest fortnight in the choral calendar and singers are juggling other work. Ask who is confirmed, and when you will know.

Who directs the group. Somebody chooses the arrangements, sets the balance in the room, decides where the singers stand, and calls the running order when the speeches overrun by twenty minutes. Ask who that person is and whether they are in the room.

Whether the group sings together regularly. Some carol groups are settled ensembles. Others are assembled per booking from a pool of freelancers. Pickup groups of good singers can be excellent, but only when the singers already know one another’s voices, so it is a fair thing to ask about.

None of this is a mark against agencies. The information sits with the act, not the platform, which is why the platform cannot publish it for you.


### What booking direct with a choir means

Going direct means the person answering your email is the person responsible for the music. With The London Choral Service, that is Luca Wetherall, our Artistic Director. He auditioned every singer on the team himself, picks the ensemble for your date, and plans the programme with you. If you want the Sussex Carol before the chairman speaks and something quiet under the mulled wine afterwards, you are discussing that with the musician who will direct it, not with a middleman relaying it.

We book ensembles from singers who have worked together wherever the December calendar allows, rather than assembling a group from whoever is free. If a singer falls ill, we replace them from within the same team instead of cancelling on you.

The other difference is the price. No intermediary layer sits inside our fee, and the figures are published rather than quoted on request. You can read them before you speak to us.


### Questions to ask, whichever route you take

These five work on an agency, a marketplace act, and a choir taking its own bookings. Ask them in writing.

- Will the singers I am looking at be the singers who perform? If the answer is that the line-up is confirmed nearer the date, ask when you will get the names and what the standard is guaranteed to be.
- Who directs the group on the night? A named director who is present is a good sign. So is a clear answer about who runs the sound check and who talks to your event manager when the timings slip.
- Can I hear this group, not a showreel? A recording of the ensemble you are booking tells you about blend and tuning. A general brand montage tells you much less.
- What does the price cover? Get the total after travel, taxes, and any booking or platform fee. Comparing a headline figure against an all-in figure flatters one of them.
- What happens if a singer is ill in December? Ask how deputies are found and whether the fee changes. Any provider working at this level should have an answer ready.

### Price transparency

Typical agency carol-group bookings run to around four figures, which is the right order of magnitude for four to six professional singers for an evening. The trouble with comparing quotes is that the headline number and the invoice number are not always the same: travel, VAT, and platform fees sit inside some quotes and outside others.

Ours are published on the pricing page . A Small Choir of four is £1,150, a quintet £1,400, a sextet £1,600, a full choir of eight £2,000, and a twelve-voice chorus £3,000; a soloist is £250. Those figures include all taxes and fees, and travel within Greater London. They do not go up for December — we charge no Christmas uplift. Christmas Eve and Christmas Day carry a premium, typically around 25 per cent, confirmed in your written quote before you commit to anything.

If you are weighing us against a quote from a platform, the useful exercise is to put both totals on the same all-in basis and then ask both providers the five questions above.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Is it cheaper to book carol singers directly or through an agency?

Not always, and anyone who promises a flat saving is guessing. Agencies price differently from one another, and what you pay turns mostly on ensemble size, the date, and how long the singers perform. What booking direct changes is transparency: there is no intermediary layer in the fee, and you can see what the money covers and who it pays. Our prices are published on our pricing page rather than quoted on request.


#### How do you know if carol singers are professional?

Ask two questions. Where did the singers train, and where do they sing for the rest of the year? The professional end of the market is staffed by conservatoire graduates and cathedral and Oxbridge choral singers who do consort work year-round. Then ask for a recording of the group you are actually booking, rather than a general showreel for the brand. Our guide to what to look for when hiring Christmas carol singers covers the rest of the checks.


#### Can I book The London Choral Service directly?

Yes. We take every booking ourselves, so there is no agency between you and the singers. Send the date, the venue, and a rough headcount through our contact page and we reply within 48 hours, usually the same day, with a written quote and two or three programme options. December dates start closing out from mid-September, so early is better.


#### What should you check before booking carol singers?

Four things. Whether the singers advertised are the singers who will perform; who directs the group on the night; what the quoted price covers once travel, taxes, and any booking fee are counted; and what happens if someone falls ill. Get the answers in writing before you pay a deposit.

Source: https://londonchoralservice.com/music-guides/how-many-carol-singers.html
Summary: How many carol singers to book for a lobby, a hall, or a church: what four, six, eight and twelve voices each cover, and why four is the smallest group.

## How many carol singers do you need?

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

The honest answer is that it depends on the ceiling more than the guest list. A room with a hard floor and height above it carries four voices further than a carpeted function suite carries eight. This guide works through the sizes we book most, what each one covers, and the point at which adding voices stops making a difference.


### Start with the room, not the headcount

Most people size a booking by the number of guests. It is the wrong first question. Two hundred people in a church with a stone floor and a high vaulted roof need fewer singers than a hundred people in a hotel function room with carpet, low ceilings and soft furnishings, because the church does half the work and the function room fights you.

What matters is how much of the sound comes back. Hard surfaces reflect it; carpet, curtains and full bookshelves absorb it. Height gives the sound somewhere to bloom before it reaches anyone. When we ask for photographs of a venue before quoting, this is what we are looking at, along with where the bar is and which direction the chatter will be coming from.

The second question is what the singers are for. A group leading congregational carols needs the strength to be heard over a room already singing, which is a different requirement from a group performing to a seated audience. Leading takes more voices than performing does.


### Why four is the smallest unaccompanied group

Carols are written in four parts: soprano, alto, tenor and bass. With four singers you have one voice on each line, which is the smallest group that can sing the harmony as written without leaving a hole in it.

Take one away and something has to give. Three voices means dropping a part or asking someone to jump between two, and the gap is usually at the bottom, which is where the sound gets its warmth. A congregation will not be able to name what is missing, but they will sing more tentatively, because the bass line is what tells people where the harmony is going.

This is why our carol bookings start with a Small Choir of four . It is not a minimum-order rule; it is the smallest group that sounds like a choir rather than like some singers.


### Four singers

Four voices in full harmony will lead a room of about 150 through Hark! The Herald Angels Sing , fill an office reception or a hotel lobby, and carry a village-scale church. This is the most common Christmas booking we take, and for most events it is the right answer.

What four singers cannot do is split. The bigger carol arrangements divide into six or eight parts, and a quartet has to sing a reduction of those instead. If your programme is built around the Willcocks descants or double-choir writing, four is where you start feeling the limit.

A Small Choir of four is £1,150, inclusive of taxes, fees and travel within Greater London.


### Six singers

Six gives you two voices doubling on the outer parts, usually the sopranos and basses. The practical effect is that the group punches through background noise: a busy hotel foyer with a bar running, a mid-sized hall, an outdoor switch-on with a crowd talking through the countdown.

Six is the size we suggest when the room is loud rather than large. Four unamplified voices can lose a fight with fifty people holding drinks; six generally win it. A Sextet is £1,600.


### Eight singers

Eight covers a large church or a full carol service with congregational hymns, and can split into eight parts for the bigger anthems. If you are booking a church that seats 400 and expect it full, this is the size that will lead the singing rather than accompany it.

Eight also gives the programme more range. Pieces that need a proper choral sound rather than a consort sound — Howells, Darke, the double-choir carols — open up here. A Full Choir of eight is £2,000.


### Twelve singers

Twelve is for cathedrals, ticketed concerts, and congregations of several hundred. At this size the choir stops being a group at the front and becomes the sound of the building. If you are selling tickets on the strength of the music, twelve is what people are picturing when they buy them.

A Chorus of twelve is £3,000. Above twelve we quote per project.


### When two or three voices work

There is one case where fewer than four makes sense: when there is an organ or piano underneath. An instrument covers the harmony the missing voices would have carried, so two or three singers over an organ can hold a chapel service that the same two or three would struggle with unaccompanied.

Priced from the standard rates, that is £250 per singer plus £225 for the organist, so £725 for two voices and organ, £975 for three. A single voice works on its own terms for a sung grace at a dinner or one set piece, at £250.

What we will not do is send two or three singers to stand in a lobby with no instrument. It does not work, and December is not the month to find that out.


### What else changes the answer

Outdoors. Open air takes the reflections away, so you lose the help the building was giving you. Add two voices to whatever the indoor answer would have been.

Roaming versus stationary. Singers moving through a crowd are only ever heard by the part of the room they are standing in, which means a smaller group can work harder. Singers performing a set to the whole room at once need to reach the back of it.

Whether the room sings. If you want a singalong on the last three carols, size up. Leading is harder than performing.

Amplification. We do not normally use it, and trained voices rarely need it. Where a venue is hostile — a shopping centre with music playing over the top — we will say so rather than send a group that cannot be heard.


### Sizing by venue type


#### Office reception or atrium

Four. Office atriums are usually hard-surfaced with height, which is the best acoustic a building can give you for free. Put the singers at the foot of a staircase or on a mezzanine and the sound reaches three floors. The only reason to go to six is if the reception runs alongside a bar and a hundred people arriving at once.


#### Hotel lobby or festive afternoon tea

Four for a tea service, six for an evening lobby. Afternoon tea rooms are quieter and the singers are working close to seated guests; an evening lobby has a bar, a concierge desk, luggage, and constant movement through it. Six voices hold that without anyone pushing their voice, which matters across a three-set evening.


#### Church carol service

Four for a church seating up to about 200, eight for one seating 400. The deciding factor is how full it will be: an empty church is a resonant one, and a full church is not, because people absorb sound. If you are expecting the building full and the congregation singing, size to the congregation rather than the architecture.


#### Livery hall or gala dinner

Four for a sung grace and a short set. Livery halls are panelled, which absorbs more than stone, but the room is usually silent when the singing starts, so you are not fighting anything. Six if the choir is performing between courses while service continues around them.


#### Apartment lobby or residents’ evening

Four. These events are usually forty to eighty residents with mulled wine, and the point is a singalong rather than a recital. Four voices and a song sheet does more here than eight voices and a programme.


#### Christmas market or light switch-on

Six at least, eight if there is a PA playing anything nearby. Outdoors removes the reflections, and a crowd outdoors is louder than the same crowd indoors. This is the one setting where under-booking is obvious to everyone present.


### Three sizing mistakes worth avoiding

Sizing to the guest list. A hundred people in a carpeted function suite is a harder room than three hundred in a church. The building decides more than the headcount does.

Booking a large group for a roaming set. Singers moving through a crowd are only heard by the part of the room they are in. Twelve voices roaming is twelve voices being heard by thirty people at a time, which is an expensive way to do what four would.

Forgetting the room fills up. Venues are quoted empty and experienced full. Coats, bodies and a carpet of conversation take a surprising amount of sound out of a room, which is why we ask what time the singing starts relative to the drinks.


### If you are not sure

Send us the venue, the date and a rough guest count, and say whether you want the room singing or listening. We will tell you which size fits and, where the smaller one would do, we will say that too. Sizing up is not always the answer, and quoting for voices a room does not need is a quick way to lose a client for next year.

Photographs help more than dimensions. What we are looking for is the floor, the ceiling height, and where the noise will be coming from. If you have a floor plan from the venue, that is better still.

Our guide to what carol singers cost sets out the full price ladder, and the pricing page covers every ensemble we offer.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Is four carol singers enough for a carol service?

For most carol services, yes. Four voices in full harmony will lead a congregation of around 150 and cover the standard carol repertoire. If you are expecting 400 in a large church, or want the choir to split into eight parts for the bigger anthems, book eight.


#### Can you book just two carol singers?

Only with an organist or pianist. Two voices cannot hold four-part harmony on their own, so unaccompanied groups start at four. Two singers with an organ is £725, priced at £250 per singer plus £225 for the organist.


#### Do more carol singers mean a wider repertoire?

Yes, from six upwards. Four singers cover the standard carols but must sing a reduction of anything written in more than four parts. Six adds weight on the outer lines, and eight can split into eight parts for double-choir pieces and the fuller descant arrangements.


#### How many carol singers fit in a hotel lobby?

Four suits most lobbies, and six if there is a bar running and a crowd talking over it. The singers need somewhere to stand together rather than a stage, and a hard floor with height above it carries the sound further than any extra voices would.

Summary: Carols that work with one voice per part: which arrangements suit a quartet, which need more singers, and how to build an hour for four voices.

## The best carols for four voices

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

A quartet is the most-booked carol ensemble there is, and most published carol arrangements were not written with one voice per part in mind. Some pieces gain from the transparency of four voices. Others collapse. This guide sorts the standard repertoire into which is which.


### What one voice per part changes

With four singers there is nowhere to hide. Every line is exposed, every entry is audible, and a single voice out of tune is not absorbed by the three others singing the same part. That cuts both ways: the texture is clearer than a larger choir can manage, and the mistakes are clearer too.

The practical consequences are worth knowing before you choose a programme. Divisi — where a part splits in two — is impossible without dropping a line. Long sustained passages are harder, because nobody can drop out to breathe without the harmony thinning. And anything relying on sheer weight of sound, the big Willcocks descant arrangements in particular, will sound underpowered however good the four singers are.

What four voices do better than eight is move. Rhythmic carols stay crisp, counterpoint stays audible, and the ensemble can follow a tempo change without a conductor.


### Carols that suit four voices


#### Ding Dong! Merrily on High

The cascading Gloria refrain is written so that the parts chase each other, and with one voice per line you can hear the chase. In a larger choir it turns into a wash.


#### The Sussex Carol

Fast, rhythmic, and dependent on the inner parts being audible. Four voices keep it light on its feet. The Willcocks arrangement is written for more, but the traditional four-part harmonisation is what most quartets sing and it loses nothing.


#### Adam Lay Ybounden

Boris Ord’s setting is barely two minutes and sits naturally in four parts. It is quiet, exposed writing, which suits a group that can hear each other properly. Programme it as the still point of a set.


#### In the Bleak Midwinter (Holst)

The Cranham setting is a hymn tune in four parts, and a quartet sings it as written. The Darke setting is a different matter — it wants a treble line with more than one voice on it, and a soprano soloist to carry the first verse.


#### Coventry Carol

Sixteenth-century writing with bare, open harmonies that were conceived for one voice per part. A large choir makes it sound thicker than it should. This is a quartet piece by design.


#### Gaudete

Unaccompanied, rhythmic, and effective with four voices in a resonant space. It also works outdoors better than most, because it does not depend on quiet dynamics surviving the open air.


### Four more that reward a quartet


#### Es ist ein Ros entsprungen (Praetorius)

The Praetorius harmonisation is four-part writing from 1609 and has never needed anything added to it. Quiet, slow, and exposed, which is why it is a good test of whether four singers are actually listening to each other. Sing it in German or in the A Spotless Rose translation, but not in both halves of the same programme.


#### Personent Hodie

Loud, rhythmic and medieval, and the four-part version keeps the drive that larger arrangements tend to smooth out. It is a useful opener for a set where you want the audience to stop talking without being asked.


#### The Holly and the Ivy

Deceptively plain. The traditional four-part harmonisation is well within a quartet, and its restraint makes a good contrast next to anything showier. Congregations will also join in on it, so it can sit on either side of the line depending on how you introduce it.


#### Tomorrow Shall Be My Dancing Day

John Gardner’s setting is written with enough independence in the parts that four voices can carry it, and the rhythm stays tighter with one on a line than with three; it needs confidence rather than numbers.


### Carols that want more than four

O Holy Night needs a soloist who can carry the climax, and a quartet leaves nobody to accompany them properly. Hark! The Herald Angels Sing with the Willcocks descant needs a treble line strong enough to sit above a congregation, which one soprano cannot do. Howells’s A Spotless Rose and most twentieth-century English carol anthems assume divisi and a choral rather than consort sound.

None of these are impossible with four voices. They are better with six or eight, and if your programme leans on them, that is a reason to size up rather than to compromise the pieces.


### Carols the room can sing over four voices

A quartet leading congregational singing is doing a different job from a quartet performing. The carols that work are the ones where the melody is strong enough to carry a room on its own: O Come, All Ye Faithful , Hark! The Herald Angels Sing , Once in Royal David’s City , Silent Night .

Four voices will lead a room of around 150 in these. Beyond that, the congregation starts to lead itself, which is fine until a verse goes wrong and there is not enough choir to pull it back.

Print the words. A quartet cannot rescue a congregation that does not know the third verse.


### Christmas songs, as opposed to carols

Most Christmas bookings want some material that is not a carol at all: the songs people associate with December rather than with Advent. Four voices handle these well, because close-harmony arrangements of popular songs were mostly written for exactly that texture.

Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas and The Christmas Song sit naturally in four parts and suit a quiet room. Winter Wonderland and Let It Snow want a bit of swing and work better standing than roaming, because the rhythm needs the four singers watching each other. White Christmas is the one clients ask for most and the one that most needs a soloist on the melody with the other three underneath, rather than four-square harmony throughout.

Our guide to a cappella Christmas songs covers this repertoire in more detail.


### Where to stand

Four singers should stand in a close arc, facing slightly inward, close enough to hear each other without effort. A quartet spread across a stage in a line will not stay together, because each singer is hearing the others late.

Put them where the room helps: a hard floor, a corner, the foot of a staircase, under a gallery. Height above the group matters more than distance from the audience. A quartet at the bottom of a stairwell will fill a building; the same quartet in the middle of a carpeted room will not reach the back of it.

For congregational carols, the singers need to be seen as well as heard. A congregation takes its timing visually more than people realise, which is why a choir tucked behind a pillar leads worse than the same choir standing in front of it.


### Building an hour for four voices

Six to eight carols fills forty-five minutes to an hour with readings between them. For a quartet, a workable shape is three or four congregational carols, three choir-only pieces chosen from the list above, and one piece most of the audience will not know.

Alternate the energy. A fast unaccompanied piece after a big congregational carol gives the room a change of texture, and gives four singers a rest from projecting. Four voices tire faster than eight, because nobody can drop out for a verse.

Open with something the room knows. A quartet has less margin than a larger choir for a shaky start, and a first carol everyone can sing covers any settling the group needs to do.

If there is an organ in the building, use it on the congregational carols and let the quartet sing the choir pieces unaccompanied. That combination covers more ground than either on its own, and an organist is £225 on top.


### Arrangements and requests

Requests are usually workable if they arrive in time. A carol we already sing needs no notice. A song that has to be arranged for four parts needs a couple of weeks, and the arrangement has to be written for one voice per line rather than adapted from a choral edition, which is a different job.

Send requests when you book rather than in the week before. December rehearsal time is the scarcest thing we have, and a piece that arrives late is a piece the quartet sight-reads.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Can four singers cover a full carol service?

Yes. Four voices in soprano, alto, tenor and bass cover the standard carol repertoire and will lead a congregation of around 150. Pieces written with divisi, or the bigger descant arrangements, are better with six or eight.


#### Which Christmas carols work best with one voice per part?

Ding Dong! Merrily on High, the Sussex Carol, Adam Lay Ybounden, the Coventry Carol, Gaudete, and Holst's setting of In the Bleak Midwinter. All were conceived for four parts, and the clarity of a quartet helps rather than hinders them.


#### Do you need a soloist as well as four singers?

Not usually. One of the four takes any solo line, which is how Once in Royal David's City is normally sung. A separate soloist is worth adding when a piece needs a voice to sit above the ensemble throughout, such as O Holy Night.

Our carol bookings start with four voices, and Luca builds the programme around your running order and the building you are singing in. If a piece you want needs more than four, we will tell you before you book rather than after.

Summary: How to plan a carols by candlelight service: the running order, which carols suit low light, fire and safety rules, and booking a choir for December.

## Carols by candlelight

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Candlelight changes what a carol service can do. It slows the room down, it makes people quieter than they would otherwise be, and it turns a programme that would read as a concert into something closer to a vigil. It also brings a set of practical constraints that catch people out, most of them to do with whether your singers can see the music.


### What candlelight actually does to a service

A church at four in the afternoon in December is already half dark. Turning the electric light off and lighting candles does two things at once: it removes most of what the audience can see, and it removes most of what they can read. Both are the point, and both need planning around.

People behave differently in low light. They talk less on the way in, they applaud less between items, and they hold still for longer. A programme that would feel slow under strip lighting works at candlelight, which is why quiet repertoire belongs here and brisk repertoire often does not.

The practical cost is that nobody can read an order of service. If the congregation is meant to sing, they will be singing from memory, and you should choose the carols accordingly.


### Choosing the carols

Split the programme into what the room sings and what the choir sings, then apply one test to the first group: could someone sing this without the words in front of them? In practice that is a short list, and it is the right list.

Silent Night , Away in a Manger , O Come, All Ye Faithful and Hark! The Herald Angels Sing are the carols most of a British congregation can manage from memory, at least for the first verse. Once in Royal David’s City works because the opening is a solo and the room only joins later.

For the choir, candlelight suits the quiet end of the repertoire. The Coventry Carol , Praetorius’s Es ist ein Ros , Boris Ord’s Adam Lay Ybounden , Howells’s A Spotless Rose , and Darke’s In the Bleak Midwinter all belong in this setting more than they belong in a bright hall. Our carols guide covers the wider repertoire.

What to avoid: anything fast enough that the singers need to watch a beat closely, and anything with an entry the choir has to find from silence in the dark.


### How the singers see the music

This is the question every candlelit service turns on, and the one most organisers have not thought about until we ask.

Choir stall lights are the best answer where the building has them, because they light the copy and not the room. Failing that, small clip-on music lights work, though they read as a row of little white dots from the nave, which some clients mind and some do not.

The other option is to programme around it: the choir sings from memory. That is a real constraint on repertoire and it needs saying at the point of booking rather than in the week before, because a piece learned from memory has to be chosen months out.

The usual compromise is a lit choir and a dark nave. The congregation experiences candlelight; the singers can see. If your building has a chancel that can be lit separately from the body of the church, that is what to ask the verger about.


### Real candles, and what most venues will allow

Church policy on naked flame varies and is not negotiable by you on the night. Ask the incumbent or the verger early, in writing, and ask specifically about handheld candles for the congregation, which is the part most often refused.

Where handheld candles are allowed, drip protectors are usually a condition, and someone has to be responsible for lighting and extinguishing them. Where they are not, candles in the windows and on the sills give most of the effect with none of the argument.

Hotels, livery halls and corporate venues almost always say no to naked flame, and their fire officer has the final word. Battery candles have improved and at ten paces in a dark room the difference is not the thing anyone remembers about the evening.


### A running order that works

An hour is right, and the shape below is one we have used many times. Adjust the readings to suit whether the service is liturgical.

- The room in darkness; a single treble or soprano begins Once in Royal David’s City unaccompanied.
- Candles lit through the first verse; choir joins for the second; congregation for the third.
- A bidding prayer or a welcome.
- Reading, then a choir carol.
- Congregational carol.
- Reading, then a choir carol.
- Congregational carol.
- Reading, then the quietest thing in the programme.
- Silent Night , sung by everyone.
- Blessing or closing words, then O Come, All Ye Faithful with the lights up.
Bringing the electric light up for the last carol is worth doing on purpose. It sends people out at a different temperature from the one they have been sitting in, and it means the final carol can be the loud one.


### Service sheets people cannot read

Print them anyway, and hand them out at the door while the lights are still up. People read the running order on the way in, then stop reading once it goes dark, which is the right way round.

Set the type larger than you would for a daytime service. Anything under twelve point is decorative rather than useful in a church lit by candles, and an older congregation will not thank you for eleven.

Put the words to the congregational carols on facing pages rather than spread across a turn. A page turn in the dark, in unison, produces a noise that lasts longer than you would think.


### Corporate and charity candlelit services

Companies and charities book candlelit services in hired churches more often than parishes do, because the setting does the work that a function room cannot. The format transfers with two changes: the readings become secular, and the appeal or the chief executive’s words go where the sermon would have been.

For a charity, the appeal belongs before the last carol rather than at the very end, so the evening finishes on singing rather than on asking. Our guide to planning a charity carol concert covers the fundraising side.

For a company, candlelight solves the problem that a carol service in a bright hall can feel like a meeting with singing. It also sets a limit on how much of the evening can be speeches, which most event managers find useful when the invitation list starts growing.


### Christmas Eve

Most people picturing carols by candlelight are picturing Christmas Eve, and that date behaves differently from the rest of December. We do sing on both the 24th and 25th, and those two dates carry a premium of around 25 per cent, confirmed in the written quote before you commit to anything.

They are also the first dates to go. If Christmas Eve is what you want, ask in the summer, not in November. Our guide on when to book Christmas entertainment covers how the month fills.


### Heating, and other things about a dark church in December

Churches are cold, and a congregation sitting still in low light gets colder than one standing and singing. Ask the verger what the heating costs to run and how long before the service it needs to go on; the answer is usually longer than you expect and the cost sometimes lands on you.

Singers need to be able to feel their hands to turn pages, and cold air changes how voices work. We ask for somewhere warm to wait before and between, which is a request about sound quality as much as comfort.

Light the way in. A dark path from the door to the pews produces exactly the problem you would expect, particularly with an older congregation.


### What we provide

Four voices will carry a candlelit church seating up to about 200; eight will carry one seating 400. Because a candlelit programme leans on quiet repertoire, the room needs to be quiet, which in practice means the singing has to be good enough to hold silence rather than fill it.

Where the building has an organ, an organist covers the congregational carols and plays before and after, at £225 on top of the choir. Where it does not, the choir sings the whole service unaccompanied, which suits this repertoire.

A Small Choir of four is £1,150 and a Full Choir of eight is £2,000, inclusive of taxes, fees and travel within Greater London.


### Frequently asked questions


#### How do the singers read music by candlelight?

Choir stall lights are the usual answer, or small clip-on music lights. The common arrangement is a lit chancel and a dark nave, so the congregation experiences candlelight while the singers can see. Singing from memory is possible but has to be agreed when you book.


#### Which carols suit a candlelit service?

For the congregation, carols people can sing without reading: Silent Night, Away in a Manger, O Come All Ye Faithful. For the choir, the quiet end of the repertoire, such as the Coventry Carol, Praetorius's Es ist ein Ros, and Darke's In the Bleak Midwinter.


#### Are real candles allowed in most venues?

Churches vary, and the decision rests with the incumbent or verger. Handheld candles for the congregation are the part most often refused. Hotels and livery halls almost always require battery candles, and their fire officer has the final word.


#### Do you sing carols by candlelight on Christmas Eve?

Yes, on both Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. Those two dates carry a premium of around 25 per cent, confirmed in your written quote before you commit. They are the first dates to go each year, so ask early.

We sing candlelit carol services in churches across London and the rest of the UK, and we will talk to the verger about lighting and rehearsal access rather than leaving you to broker it.

Summary: Booking carol singers outdoors: how many voices a market or switch-on needs, what weather and cold do to singing, and what to provide on the day.

## Outdoor carol singing

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Outdoors takes away the thing a building was giving you for free. There are no reflections, no ceiling to hold the sound, and usually a crowd making more noise than the same crowd would make indoors. Carol singing still works out there, and we do a lot of it every December, but it is sized and planned differently.


### Why outdoor bookings need more voices

Indoors, a good part of what an audience hears is sound that has bounced off a wall or a floor. Outdoors that is gone, so the audience hears only what reaches them directly. The practical effect is that a group which fills a church can sound thin in a market square.

Add two voices to whatever the indoor answer would have been. Six is the realistic minimum for a market or a switch-on; eight if there is a public address system nearby or a crowd of several hundred.

The other half of the problem is that outdoor crowds are louder. People stand further apart, they raise their voices to be heard, and there is usually traffic. A sextet at £1,600 or a full choir of eight at £2,000 carries over that noise in a way a quartet cannot.


### Where to put the singers

Look for anything that gives sound something to come off. A shop front, a wall behind the group, an arch, a bandstand, the recess of a church porch. Singers standing in the open with nothing behind them are working twice as hard for half the result.

Corners are better than the middle of a square. A raised position helps, not because the sound travels further but because it clears the heads of the people standing at the front.

Keep the group tight. Outdoors, singers who cannot hear each other drift apart in pitch and time, and there is no acoustic to blend them back together.


### Weather, and what we ask for

Cover from rain is not negotiable. Sheet music and water do not mix, and once copies are wet the booking is over. An awning, a gazebo, a porch or a shop doorway all work; a promise that it probably will not rain does not.

Wind is the underrated problem. It takes sound away, it turns pages, and it makes it hard for singers to hear each other. Pegs and folders help; a sheltered position helps more.

We also ask for somewhere warm to wait between sets. In hard frost we would rather sing shorter sets more often than have a group stand outside for a solid hour, and that is a decision about how the last set sounds rather than about comfort.


### What the cold does to singing

Cold air is dry, and dry air is hard on voices. Singers warm up before they start and need to stay warm between sets, or the second half of an evening is measurably worse than the first.

Cold hands make page turns slow and unreliable, which is a real constraint on how complicated the repertoire can be. Outdoor programmes lean on music the group knows well for that reason.

Twenty minutes of singing followed by twenty minutes inside is a better shape for a longer outdoor booking than an hour straight through, and it produces a better result at the end of the evening.


### Repertoire that works outdoors

Choose robust over subtle. Quiet dynamics do not survive open air, and neither does anything relying on a hushed final chord. What works is rhythmic, strong-melody writing that people recognise within a bar.

Ding Dong! Merrily on High , Gaudete , Personent Hodie , The Sussex Carol , O Come, All Ye Faithful and Hark! The Herald Angels Sing are the backbone of most outdoor sets. Add a few of the popular Christmas songs for a market crowd, who are shopping rather than attending a concert.

Leave the Howells and the Darke indoors. They are written for a resonance that a street does not have.


### Switch-ons and countdowns

A light switch-on has a fixed moment in it, and the music has to arrive at that moment rather than near it. We need to know who is running the countdown, what the cue is, and whether the choir sings up to it or starts after it.

The usual shape is sets before the switch-on to build a crowd, a pause for the countdown and whatever speeches come with it, then one carol immediately afterwards while everybody is still together. The crowd disperses fast after a switch-on, so anything you want heard should come before it.

If there is a PA for the speeches, ask whether the choir can use it for that one carol. We do not normally need amplification, but a public square immediately after a countdown is the exception.


### Christmas markets and shopping streets

Market bookings are usually two to three short sets across an afternoon rather than one continuous performance, because the audience is moving through rather than standing still. Twenty minutes on, twenty off, repeated, works better than an hour of singing to people walking past.

The competing sound is the thing to check before booking. A market with its own PA playing Christmas music over the top is a venue where live singing will lose, and no ensemble size fixes it. That needs settling with the market operator, not with us.

Shopping centres are indoors but behave like outdoor spaces: hard surfaces, high ceilings and a lot of ambient noise, plus background music that someone has to agree to turn off.


### Getting a crowd to stop walking

An outdoor audience has not bought a ticket and owes you nothing. People stop because something catches them in the first few seconds, so the opening carol of every set should be one they recognise immediately and it should start at full strength rather than easing in.

Once a small group has gathered, more people join it, because a crowd is itself the advertisement. This is why three shorter sets usually draw more listeners across an afternoon than one long one: each start pulls a new group in.

Face the direction people are coming from. It sounds obvious and it is regularly got wrong when a group is positioned for a photograph rather than for an audience.


### Timings across a December afternoon

Light matters more than the clock. Most outdoor bookings are strongest between about three and six, when it is dark enough for the lights to register but early enough that families are still out.

A standard booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks, which outdoors usually means three sets of twenty to twenty-five minutes. Longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront in writing.

Tell us the switch-on time or the busiest hour when you enquire, and we will build the sets around it rather than spreading them evenly across the afternoon.


### Power, staging and licences

We need none of the first two. Everything is sung unaccompanied, so there is no power to find, nothing to plug in and no stage to build. Somewhere to stand is the whole requirement.

Where a venue has no piano and you want one, we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in the written quote. Outdoors this is rarely worth it.

Permissions are the organiser’s side of the arrangement: street trading or busking rules, council permissions for public land, and any licence the venue needs for live music. We will tell you what we need in order to sing; we do not obtain permissions on your behalf.


### Dress

Outdoors the singers wear coats, and that is the honest answer. Concert dress under a warm coat, all black, ordinary clothes for a market, or Christmas jumpers if you want the group to look festive. We have Santa hats if you want them.

Costume is the one outdoor request we turn down. We send singers, not a tableau.


### Frequently asked questions


#### How many carol singers do you need outdoors?

More than indoors. Six is the realistic minimum for a market or a switch-on, and eight where there is a public address system nearby or a crowd of several hundred. Open air removes the reflections a building would give you, so the audience hears only what reaches them directly.


#### Can carol singers perform in the rain?

Not without cover. Sheet music and water do not mix, and once copies are wet the booking cannot continue. An awning, gazebo, porch or shop doorway is enough. Cold on its own is workable, provided there is somewhere warm to wait between sets.


#### Do outdoor carol singers need amplification?

Usually not. Trained voices carry a market or a courtyard unamplified if the group is positioned against a wall or a shop front rather than in open ground. The exception is a public square straight after a switch-on countdown, where using the existing PA for one carol helps.


#### How long can carol singers sing outdoors?

A standard booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks. Outdoors we would rather split that into shorter sets with warm breaks between them than sing straight through, because cold air affects how the later sets sound.

We sing at markets, light switch-ons and street events across London and the rest of the UK. Tell us where the singers would stand and what else is making noise nearby, and we will tell you what size group the space needs.
