Summary: The Christmas songs that work unaccompanied: close-harmony standards, what suits four voices, and how to mix songs with carols at a party or reception.

## A cappella Christmas songs for a choir

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Not every Christmas booking wants carols. A drinks reception, an office party or a hotel lobby usually wants the songs people associate with December rather than with Advent, and most of those were written for exactly the close-harmony texture a small choir provides. This guide covers what works unaccompanied, and what does not.


### Songs and carols are different jobs

A carol has a congregation in mind. It is written to be sung by people who are not singers, in unison, with harmony underneath. A Christmas song is written to be listened to, usually by one voice with a band behind it, and turning it into something four unaccompanied singers can perform means rebuilding it.

That rebuilding is why some songs land and others fall flat. The ones that work have strong harmonic movement that voices can carry on their own. The ones that fail are the ones whose appeal is mostly in the arrangement: the horn section, the sleigh bells, the production.

The practical test is whether you can hum the chord changes as well as the tune. If the song is only a melody, four voices will expose that.


### The close-harmony standards


#### Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas

The most reliable song on the list. The harmony moves constantly, which gives the inner parts something to do, and it works at the quiet end of a room without dropping below what people can hear. Good early in an evening, before the volume in the room climbs.


#### The Christmas Song (Chestnuts Roasting)

Written for a singer with a jazz harmony underneath, and that harmony transfers to voices cleanly. It needs an alto and tenor who are comfortable with close intervals, and it wants a soloist on the melody rather than four-square block harmony.


#### White Christmas

The song clients ask for most. It works, but only as a solo with three voices underneath; sung as four equal parts it turns into a hymn. Give the melody to one singer and let the others move.


#### Winter Wonderland

Swing rhythm, and it needs the group standing still and watching each other rather than roaming. The rhythm is the whole appeal, and roaming singers cannot keep it tight.


#### Let It Snow

Similar territory, and a good closer for a set because it ends on an upbeat rather than a fade. Works well as the last thing before a break.


#### Santa Claus Is Comin’ to Town

The one that gets a room joining in without being asked. Not subtle, and it does not need to be.


### Songs that need more than four voices

Do You Hear What I Hear builds towards a climax that four voices cannot supply; it wants six at least. All I Want for Christmas Is You depends on rhythmic drive and a big final chorus, and unaccompanied it usually sounds like a good idea that did not survive the arrangement.

Fairytale of New York comes up in almost every enquiry. It was written for two characterful voices trading lines over a band, and choral arrangements of it flatten exactly what people like about it. We will sing it if you want it, but it is worth knowing what it becomes.

Last Christmas works better than people expect, because the chord sequence is doing most of the work and voices can carry that.


### Mixing songs and carols in one set

Most bookings want both. The mix that works is roughly two-thirds carols to one-third songs for a church or a formal service, and the reverse for a party or a lobby.

Do not alternate them one for one. Group two or three carols, then two or three songs, so the set has a shape rather than a wobble. Moving between a fifteenth-century carol and a swing standard every three minutes asks a lot of a group and gives an audience no thread to follow.

The transition works better going from old to new than the other way round. A set that opens with Gaudete and finishes with Let It Snow makes sense to a room; the reverse sounds like the programme ran out of order.


### What four unaccompanied voices can and cannot do

Four voices cover this repertoire well, because close-harmony writing is four-part writing by convention. One voice takes the melody and three move underneath, which is how these songs were arranged for vocal groups in the first place.

What four cannot do is provide both a soloist and a full backing texture at the same time. When the melody sits out on its own, you are hearing three voices of harmony, and in a busy room that thins out. Six is the answer where a booking is mostly songs rather than carols and the room is loud.

See our guide to the best carols for four voices for the same question applied to the carol repertoire.


### Arrangements, and asking for a specific song

We hold arrangements of the standard repertoire. Anything outside it has to be arranged for the specific group, which takes a couple of weeks and needs to be commissioned when you book rather than in the fortnight before.

An arrangement written for one voice per part is not the same as a choral edition with the parts thinned out. The former is written knowing exactly who is singing each line; the latter usually leaves the texture with holes in it. This matters more for songs than for carols, because song arrangements lean harder on the inner voices.

If a particular song matters to you — a first dance, a company anthem, something with a history — say so at the point of enquiry. December rehearsal time is the scarcest resource we have.


### Where these songs suit the room

Drinks receptions. Songs work better than carols here. Guests are talking, arriving across an hour, and not expecting to sing along. Close harmony sits under conversation in a way a congregational carol does not.

Seated dinners. Quiet songs between courses, with the group positioned away from the tables. This is where Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas and The Christmas Song earn their place.

Hotel lobbies and afternoon teas. A mix, weighted towards songs, with the well-known carols kept for the end of each set when people have gathered.

Church services. Carols, with at most one song, and only if the incumbent is content. A carol service is not the place to discover that the vicar has views about Santa Claus Is Comin’ to Town .


### The folk and traditional end

Between the carols proper and the twentieth-century songs sits a body of traditional material that suits unaccompanied voices better than either. The Wexford Carol , The Cherry Tree Carol , Down in Yon Forest and the Appalachian I Wonder as I Wander are modal, unhurried, and were sung without accompaniment long before anyone arranged them.

These are useful in a set that is otherwise light, because they change the temperature without slowing the room down the way a Howells anthem would. They also suit a smaller group: four voices is plenty, and in some cases a solo verse with three voices humming underneath is closer to how the material was meant to sound.

The Coventry Carol belongs in this group as much as in the carol repertoire, and it is the one piece we would put in almost any Christmas set regardless of the setting.


### Sets, breaks and how long a group can sing

A standard Christmas booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks, which in practice is three sets of about twenty minutes. Unaccompanied singing is more tiring than singing with an instrument, because there is nothing to rest against and the group is holding its own pitch throughout.

Where a venue has a piano, booking a pianist to cover the gaps keeps the room from falling silent between sets and gives the singers a genuine rest. The pianist plays through the break and drops out as the voices come back in. That is £225 on top of the singers.

If the venue has no piano at all we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in your written quote. For a booking that is mostly songs rather than carols, it is usually worth it.


### Licensing

Most of these songs are still in copyright, and live performance of copyright music at a public event is normally covered by the venue’s own licence. Hotels, function venues and shopping centres almost always hold one. Churches often do not, because their usual repertoire does not need it.

For a private event on private premises the position is different again. Check with your venue rather than assuming, and if you are selling tickets, check before you sell them.

This is one of the practical reasons a church booking tends to be carols rather than songs, and it is worth knowing before you build a programme around Last Christmas .


### Frequently asked questions


#### Which Christmas songs work a cappella?

The close-harmony standards: Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas, The Christmas Song, White Christmas, Winter Wonderland, Let It Snow. These have enough harmonic movement for voices to carry on their own, rather than depending on a band arrangement.


#### Can four singers perform Christmas songs without a piano?

Yes. Close-harmony writing is four-part writing by convention, with one voice on the melody and three moving underneath. Six is better where the booking is mostly songs and the room is noisy, because the backing texture thins when the melody sits out alone.


#### Will you sing a specific Christmas song on request?

Usually, if it reaches us in time. Songs already in our repertoire need no notice. Anything else has to be arranged for the specific group, which takes a couple of weeks and should be commissioned when you book rather than in the fortnight before.


#### Should a Christmas programme be songs or carols?

Both, weighted to the setting. Roughly two-thirds carols for a church or a formal service, and the reverse for a party, reception or hotel lobby. Group them in threes rather than alternating, so the set has a shape.

We sing carols and close-harmony Christmas songs at parties, receptions and lobbies across the UK. Tell us the room and the tone you are after, and Luca sets the running order against it.

Summary: For parishes and schools without a choir of their own: what hiring singers for a carol service involves, what it costs, and how it works with your organist.

## Hiring a choir for a church carol service

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Plenty of churches want a proper carol service and no longer have the singers to do it. A hired choir fills that gap for one evening a year, and the arrangement is more straightforward than most incumbents expect. This guide covers what to book, how it fits alongside whatever musical resources you already have, and what it costs.


### Who this suits

Parishes whose choir has shrunk to three or four faithful singers. Churches with a good organ and nobody to sing over it. Schools holding a carol service in a church they have hired. Chaplaincies, colleges and livery companies who use a City church once a year and need it to sound like the building deserves.

In each case the need is the same: one evening where the singing carries the service rather than the congregation having to hold it up on their own.

What we do not do is replace a parish choir. Where there is an existing choir, the usual arrangement is that we sing alongside them, which is covered further down.


### What size the church needs

Four voices will lead a congregation of about 150 and cover the standard carol repertoire in full harmony. This is the right answer for most parish churches and it is where our carol bookings start, at £1,150.

Eight covers a church seating 400 with a full congregation, and can split into eight parts for the bigger anthems — the Willcocks arrangements, Howells, the double-choir carols. A Full Choir of eight is £2,000.

Twelve is for cathedral-scale buildings and ticketed concerts, at £3,000. Between those, a Quintet is £1,400 and a Sextet £1,600.

Size to the congregation you expect rather than to the architecture. A large church half full is a resonant space that flatters a small group; the same church full of people in winter coats absorbs a surprising amount of sound.


### Working with your own organist

If you have an organist, keep them. They know the instrument, they know the building, and an organ is idiosyncratic enough that familiarity matters more than most clergy realise. We send singers and they play, which is the cheapest and usually the best arrangement.

What the choir needs from your organist is a copy of the hymn and carol list a few weeks out, and agreement on which verses are harmonised, which are in unison, and where any descants fall. Those decisions are quick to make and expensive to improvise on the night.

Where your organist is already committed that week, or the post is vacant, we can provide one at £225 on top of the choir booking. Say early which it is, because December organists go at least as fast as December singers.


### Singing alongside an existing parish choir

This works, and it is a common arrangement, but it needs deciding in advance rather than on the night. The two options are that our singers stiffen the existing parts, or that the two choirs sing different items.

Stiffening the parts means our singers sit within the existing choir, one to a line, and hold it up from inside. It is the better option where the parish choir is small but willing, and it tends to be the more generous-feeling arrangement for the people who sing every week.

Splitting the items means the parish choir keeps the carols it knows and our singers take the harder pieces alone. This suits a service where you want two or three anthems the existing choir could not attempt.

Either way, tell your choir before we arrive. A hired choir turning up unannounced at a parish carol service is a pastoral problem, not a musical one, and it is entirely avoidable.


### Nine Lessons and Carols, or something shorter

The King’s College pattern — bidding prayer, nine readings, a carol after each, a blessing — runs to about an hour and is what most people mean by a carol service. Our guide to Nine Lessons and Carols sets out the full order.

Nine readings is a lot for a small congregation, and there is no obligation. Five or six readings with carols between them makes a service of about forty-five minutes that holds attention better in a cold church.

Whatever the length, agree early which carols the congregation sings and which the choir takes alone. Six of each is the usual balance for an hour. That single decision shapes the rehearsal, the service sheet, and how the evening feels more than any other choice you will make.


### Rehearsal and access

Our singers rehearse before they arrive; what we need at the church is time in the building to balance the sound and to work with the organ. Thirty to forty-five minutes before the doors open is enough for a standard service.

That has to be agreed with whoever holds the keys. Vergers control access, heating and lighting, and in a busy December a church may have something else in it two hours before your service. Once a booking is confirmed we contact the verger and the organist directly and send you the times, rather than asking you to relay messages.

If any liturgy is involved, the incumbent will want to see the order of service. Send it to them before you print it.


### Heating, and the cold

Ask what the heating costs to run and how long it needs. Churches take hours to warm and the answer is often a bigger line in the budget than people anticipate.

It matters musically too. Cold air is hard on voices and cold hands turn pages badly, so a church heated from an hour before produces a better service than one heated from twenty minutes before. Somewhere warm for the singers to wait is a request about the sound as much as about comfort.


### What it costs, and what is included

The figure quoted covers the singers, the programme planning, the rehearsal, the music, and the coordination with your organist and verger. Prices include all taxes and fees and travel within Greater London; travel beyond that is quoted with the booking.

A standard booking covers the length of a church service. There is no Christmas uplift: December is charged at the same rates as the rest of the year. The exceptions are Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, which carry a premium of around 25 per cent, confirmed in writing before you commit.

For a parish weighing this against a year of choir costs, one hired evening is a different kind of spend from maintaining a choir, and it is worth being clear internally which of the two the PCC thinks it is buying.


### When to ask

December dates go by the middle of September most years, and the third weekend of December is the tightest window in the calendar. Churches that hold the same slot annually should rebook as soon as the date is fixed.

Later enquiries are always worth making, because the right combination of singers is sometimes still free. Send the date and we will confirm availability the same day. Our guide on when to book Christmas entertainment sets out how the month fills.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Can a church hire a choir for one carol service?

Yes, and it is a common booking. Parishes without a choir of their own, or with a choir too small to lead a full congregation, hire singers for a single evening in December. The fee covers the singers, the rehearsal, the music and coordination with your organist and verger.


#### Will a hired choir sing with our existing parish choir?

Either arrangement works. Our singers can sit within the existing choir to hold up the parts from inside, or the two choirs can split the items so the parish choir keeps the carols it knows and ours take the harder pieces. Decide which in advance, and tell your choir.


#### Do we need to provide an organist?

Keep yours if you have one, since they know the instrument and the building. If the post is vacant or your organist is committed elsewhere that week, we can provide one from £225 on top of the choir booking. December organists book up as fast as singers, so say early which you need.


#### How much does it cost for a church to hire a carol service choir?

Four singers is £1,150 and eight is £2,000, inclusive of taxes, fees and travel within Greater London. December is charged at the same rates as the rest of the year, with a premium of around 25 per cent on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day only.

We sing carol services in parish churches, school chapels and City churches across the UK, and we deal with your verger and organist directly once the booking is confirmed.

Summary: How live music works at a Christmas drinks reception: when the singing should start, roaming or stationary sets, how loud is right, and what it costs.

## Music for a Christmas drinks reception

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

A drinks reception is the hardest room a choir sings in, and the one they are booked for most. Guests arrive across an hour, nobody is seated, nobody has come to listen, and the volume climbs steadily as the wine goes round. Music that works here is planned around those facts rather than in spite of them.


### What the music is actually for

At a concert the audience is there for the performance. At a drinks reception the performance is there for the audience, and its job is to change the room rather than to hold it. That distinction decides everything else: the repertoire, the volume, where the singers stand, and when they start.

The measurable effect is on how people behave when they walk in. A room with live singing in it is a room guests enter differently: they arrive already in an occasion rather than in a corridor with drinks. Most of the value is spent in the first fifteen minutes, which is why the singing should be underway before the first guest arrives, not after.

The second effect is on the shape of the evening. Live music gives a reception punctuation — a beginning, a moment where people gather, an end — that a playlist does not provide, because nobody notices a playlist stopping.


### Start before the doors open

The single most common mistake is booking the singers from the same time as the invitation. Guests then arrive to a group setting up, which reverses the effect you paid for.

Have the choir singing from fifteen minutes before the stated start. Early arrivals, who are usually the most senior people in the room, walk into something already happening. It also gives the group time to settle the balance in a room that is still quiet.

The corollary is at the other end: stop before the room does. A choir singing to eleven remaining guests is a choir that stayed too long.


### Roaming or stationary

Roaming suits a reception where guests arrive across an hour and the room has more than one focus — several bars, an exhibition, adjoining spaces. The singers move between groups, stop where people have gathered, and take the atmosphere with them. Nobody hears the whole programme, and nobody minds.

Stationary sets suit a reception with a moment in it: a speech, a toast, a sponsor to thank, an appeal. Singers in a fixed position give the room somewhere to face, which makes the transition into the formal part of the evening much easier for whoever is running it.

Most bookings use both. Roaming while guests arrive, then a stationary set of three or four pieces at the point where you want everyone in one place, then back to roaming. Tell us where the speeches fall and we will build the sets around them.


### How loud, and how close

The mistake in the other direction is music that is too present. A reception where guests have to raise their voices to talk over the singing is one where the music has become an obstacle, and clients notice that in the feedback even when they cannot name the cause.

Distance is the control. Singers positioned at the edge of a room, on a staircase, or in an adjoining space with the doors open give the sound room to arrive as atmosphere rather than as an announcement. Singers in the middle of the floor become the event whether or not that is what you wanted.

Everything is sung unaccompanied, so there is no volume control to get wrong and nothing to plug in. Trained voices are also better at singing quietly than any amplified source, which is the property that makes this work at all.


### Repertoire for a room that is talking

Weight the programme towards close-harmony Christmas songs rather than carols. Guests at a reception are not expecting to sing, and a congregational carol invites participation the room is not set up for. Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas , The Christmas Song and Winter Wonderland do the work here; our guide to a cappella Christmas songs covers the repertoire in full.

Keep two or three well-known carols for the stationary set, when people are gathered and facing the singers. That is where O Come, All Ye Faithful earns its place, and where a room will join in if you want it to.

Avoid the quiet end of the choral repertoire. Howells and Darke are written for a silent church, and a reception is not one. Putting them in a drinks set wastes the pieces and exposes the singers.


### Sizing the group to the room

Four voices cover a reception of up to about 150 in a room with hard surfaces. Six is the answer where there is a bar running, a room of 200 or more, or an atrium with several floors of noise coming into it.

Receptions are louder than their headcount suggests, because everyone is standing and talking at once. If in doubt at the margin, six is the safer booking; four singers straining to be heard across a busy room is not a better version of the same thing.

A Small Choir of four is £1,150 and a Sextet is £1,600, inclusive of taxes, fees and travel within Greater London. Our guide on how many carol singers you need works through the sizing in more detail.


### Where to put them

Look for height and a hard floor. A staircase, a gallery, a mezzanine, the corner of an atrium. Anywhere the sound can rise and spread before it reaches anyone is better than the middle of the room.

Avoid three places: next to the bar, next to the entrance, and next to the kitchen doors. Each has its own noise, and the first two are also where the room is most congested.

Singers need nothing but somewhere to stand. No power, no stage, no PA. If your venue offers a stage, it is usually worth declining it, because a stage tells guests to stop and watch, which is not what a reception set is doing.


### Piano between the sets

Where the venue has a piano, booking a pianist to cover the gaps is worth the money. The pianist plays through the breaks and drops out as the singers come back in, so the room never falls silent and the sets stop feeling like separate performances.

A pianist is £225 on top of the singers. If the venue has no piano and you want one, we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront in the written quote.

This is the addition we recommend most often for receptions running longer than ninety minutes, because unaccompanied singing is tiring and the alternative is longer breaks in silence.


### Timings and cost

A standard Christmas booking runs up to an hour and a half including breaks, which is usually three sets of twenty minutes or continuous singing across a shorter reception. Longer bookings carry a premium, quoted upfront in writing.

Ninety minutes covers most drinks receptions comfortably. If the reception runs into a dinner, that is a longer booking and a different shape, and worth saying at the enquiry stage.

December is charged at the same rates as the rest of the year, with a premium of around 25 per cent on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day only. Dates go by the middle of September in most years.


### Dress

Concert dress for a formal evening, all black where the singers should not draw the eye, ordinary clothes for something relaxed, or Christmas jumpers if you want the group to look like part of the party. Santa hats are available if you ask.

For a client-facing reception, all black is the safe answer. It reads as staff rather than as entertainment, which is usually the right register when the guests are customers.


### Frequently asked questions


#### When should singers start at a drinks reception?

Fifteen minutes before the stated start time, so early arrivals walk into something already happening rather than into a group setting up. Most of the effect is spent in the first fifteen minutes, and it also lets the singers settle the balance while the room is quiet.


#### Should carol singers roam or stay in one place at a reception?

Usually both. Roaming suits guests arriving across an hour and rooms with more than one focus. A stationary set works where there is a speech or a toast, because it gives the room somewhere to face. Tell us where the speeches fall and we build the sets around them.


#### Will live singing be too loud for guests to talk?

Not if the group is positioned at the edge of the room, on a staircase, or in an adjoining space. Everything is sung unaccompanied, and trained voices are better at singing quietly than any amplified source. Singers in the middle of the floor become the event; singers at the edge change the atmosphere.


#### How many singers for a Christmas drinks reception?

Four covers a reception of up to about 150 in a room with hard surfaces. Six suits a room of 200 or more, an atrium, or a reception with a busy bar. Receptions are louder than their headcount suggests, because everyone is standing and talking at once.

Summary: Live music at a seated Christmas dinner: a sung grace, set pieces between courses, working around speeches and awards, and what each option costs.

## Music for a Christmas gala or awards dinner

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

A seated dinner is a fixed running order with other people’s speeches in it, and music at one succeeds or fails on timing rather than on repertoire. The pieces are short, the moments are specific, and the whole thing has to survive a starter arriving late. This guide covers the three places music usually goes and how to brief the room.


### Three places music goes at a dinner

The grace. A sung grace before the meal is the oldest of these and still the most effective. One voice, unaccompanied, thirty seconds, and the room goes from two hundred people talking to complete silence without anyone tapping a glass.

Between courses. Short set pieces while plates are cleared. Two or three minutes each, no more, and placed where the service has a natural pause rather than where your running order says it should be.

After the loyal toast or the awards. A longer set once the formal business is done and before the room breaks up. This is where a choir can actually perform, because for the first time in the evening nobody is eating.

Most dinners use one or two of these. Using all three is possible and needs the toastmaster on side from the start.


### The sung grace

A single trained voice silences a room faster than a microphone does, which is the practical argument for a sung grace at a large dinner. It also solves the problem of a chairman having to shout for attention before their own event has started.

Latin graces are the tradition in livery halls, colleges and City dinners, and they have the advantage of brevity. An English grace suits a corporate audience better where nobody is expecting Latin, and a bespoke grace naming the company or the occasion is straightforward to arrange if you ask in advance.

A soloist is £250. This is the cheapest thing on the list and the one that most reliably gets remarked on.


### Between courses

Keep them short. Two or three minutes is right; five is too long for a room that has just been served. The pieces should be self-contained, recognisable within a bar, and not require the audience to have heard the previous one.

Placement is the hard part, because kitchens run to their own timetable. The workable arrangement is that we agree the pieces in advance and the toastmaster or banqueting manager cues them on the night, rather than fixing them to clock times that will drift by twenty minutes before the main course.

The singers should be positioned away from the tables, ideally at one end of the room or on a gallery. Close to the tables, a choir makes the guests nearest to them stop eating, which is not a kindness.

Expect service to continue during the music at all but the most formal dinners. That is normal, and it is a reason to choose robust pieces over delicate ones.


### Working around speeches and awards

An awards dinner has a lot of talking in it, and music is the thing that stops it becoming an unbroken hour of it. Placed between award categories, a two-minute piece resets the room’s attention, which is worth more at that point in the evening than anything on the menu.

What to avoid is music immediately after a long speech, when the room wants to talk. Better before the speeches than after them, or between two of them rather than at the end of the run.

If there is a charity appeal, put the music before it rather than after. A room that has just listened to something sung together gives more than a room that has just sat through the third speech.

We need the running order a week out, and we need to know who holds the cue on the night. A dinner where nobody has been told to signal the choir is a dinner where the choir sings at the wrong moment.


### Ensemble size for a dinner

Dinner rooms are more forgiving than receptions, because the audience is seated and the room falls quiet on cue. Four voices cover a dinner of up to about 200; six for a large banqueting hall or a room of 300 and above.

For a grace alone, one voice is the right answer and a choir is not an improvement. A soloist singing a grace to five hundred people works, because the room is silent by design.

Livery halls are usually panelled, which absorbs more sound than stone but presents no real difficulty when the room is quiet. Hotel ballrooms have height and hard surfaces and carry sound well. Marquees are the hardest room of the three and want six voices.

A Small Choir of four is £1,150, a Sextet £1,600, and a soloist £250.


### Repertoire for a seated room

Carols work better at a dinner than at a reception, because the room is quiet and facing one direction. Two or three well-known carols in the after-dinner set will get a seated room singing where the same carols at a drinks reception would not.

For between courses, close-harmony Christmas songs sit better than sacred repertoire: they are shorter, they carry over the sound of service, and they do not ask the room to change mood mid-meal.

The after-dinner set is where the choral repertoire earns its place. This is the point to programme the piece the choir does best, because it is the only part of the evening with the room’s full attention.

Finish on something everyone knows. A dinner that ends with the room singing breaks up in a better temper than one that ends with applause.


### Practical requirements

Singers need somewhere to stand and somewhere to wait. A holding room matters more at a dinner than anywhere else, because the group may be on site for three hours and singing for twenty minutes of them.

Everything is sung unaccompanied, so there is no power requirement and nothing to plug in. Where a venue has a piano and you want background music between the sets, a pianist is £225 on top of the choir booking; if there is no piano we can bring a keyboard and speaker for an extra charge, quoted upfront.

Tell us whether the singers are eating. It is a small thing and it is the question banqueting managers most often forget to ask, and a group that has been on site since six without a meal does not sing better at ten.


### Dress and register

Black tie dinners want concert dress. All black is the alternative where the choir should read as part of the evening rather than as a turn. Christmas jumpers do not belong at a gala dinner, and we will say so if you ask for them.

For a City or livery dinner, the register is formal throughout: a Latin grace, restrained repertoire, and singers who understand that they are part of the proceedings rather than the entertainment. Our page for livery companies covers that setting specifically.


### Booking

The corporate dinner season runs from late November to the third week of December, and the Thursdays in that window go first. Most years our December dates are gone by the middle of September.

December is charged at the same rates as the rest of the year. A standard booking covers up to an hour and a half including breaks; a dinner where the choir is on call across a four-hour running order is a longer booking, and we quote that upfront rather than adding it afterwards.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What is a sung grace and how long does it take?

A short grace sung before the meal, usually by one voice and unaccompanied, lasting around thirty seconds. It silences a large dining room faster than a microphone, which is why livery companies and City dinners still use it. A soloist is £250.


#### How long should music between dinner courses last?

Two or three minutes per piece. Five is too long for a room that has just been served. Pieces should be self-contained and cued by the toastmaster or banqueting manager on the night, rather than fixed to clock times that drift as the kitchen runs.


#### Where should music go in an awards dinner running order?

Between award categories rather than after a long speech, because a short piece resets the room's attention. If there is a charity appeal, put the music before it: a room that has just sung together gives more than one that has sat through three speeches.


#### How many singers for a Christmas gala dinner?

Four covers a dinner of up to about 200, and six suits a large banqueting hall or a room of 300 and above. Marquees are the hardest of the three rooms and want six. For a sung grace on its own, one voice is the right answer.

We sing at Christmas gala dinners, awards evenings and livery hall banquets across the UK, from a sung grace to a full after-dinner set. Send us the running order and we will tell you where the music should sit in it.

## Carol singers for law firms and professional services

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: August 2026

Professional services firms book more carol singing than any other sector we work with, and they book it for a specific reason: December is when clients are entertained, and a choir in an atrium is one of the few things at a client event that nobody has to be persuaded to enjoy. This guide covers how those bookings usually work.


### Why this sector books carols

Client entertaining in December has a problem: everyone is doing it, the invitations compete, and a drinks party in a City office is much like a drinks party in the office next door. Live singing is a cheap way to be the one people remember, and unlike most differentiators it works on the guests who arrive already tired of Christmas parties.

The second reason is internal. A firm with several floors, several departments and a lot of people who do not meet each other has a real problem making a Christmas event feel like one occasion. A choir in the atrium pulls people out of their floors in a way an email does not.

The third is continuity. Firms rebook the same evening year after year, and after two or three years it stops being an event and becomes a fixture that clients ask about. That is worth more than the sum of the individual evenings.


### The events firms book

Client drinks in the office. The most common by far. Singers roaming while guests arrive, a stationary set at the point the senior partner speaks, then roaming again. Our guide to Christmas drinks reception music covers the shape in detail.

The partners’ dinner. A seated dinner, usually with a sung grace and a short set after the meal. Covered in our guide to gala and awards dinner music .

A carol service in a City church. Firms with a long-standing church relationship hire it for an evening, invite clients and families, and want an eight-voice choir and an organist. This is the most formal option and the one that reads best on an invitation.

Atrium or reception carols with no event attached. An hour at lunchtime or at the end of the day, for staff rather than clients, with no speeches. The cheapest thing on this list and the one with the best internal feedback per pound.


### Sizing an office building

Modern City offices have good acoustics by accident. Atriums are hard-surfaced with height, glass reflects, and stone or polished concrete floors do the rest. Four voices at the foot of an atrium staircase will reach several floors.

Where it gets harder is a carpeted client-floor reception with a low ceiling, which is acoustically the opposite. Six voices there, or move the singers to the stairwell and let the sound come through.

For a church service, four covers a congregation of 150 and eight covers 400. City churches are small: St Bride’s, St Lawrence Jewry and their neighbours are not cathedrals, and eight voices in one of them is a substantial sound.

A Small Choir of four is £1,150, a Sextet £1,600, and a Full Choir of eight £2,000.


### Working with building management

Most City firms do not control their own building. Singing in a shared atrium means clearing it with the managing agent as well as with your own facilities team, and that conversation takes longer in December than anyone plans for.

The questions that come up are always the same: how loud, for how long, does it need power, and does it need a licence. The answers are that it is unamplified, up to ninety minutes including breaks, no power at all, and licensing is the building’s question rather than ours. Nothing needs to be plugged in and there is no stage to build.

Security and access lists matter more here than at other venues. We send names and arrival times once the booking is confirmed, and we would rather do that two weeks out than on the morning.


### Client-facing register

All black is the right dress for a client event. It reads as professional rather than as a turn, which matters when the guests are customers and the firm is trying to look like a firm. Concert dress suits a church service or a formal dinner. Christmas jumpers work for a staff-only event and rarely for a client one.

Repertoire follows the same logic. Client drinks want close-harmony Christmas songs and the well-known carols, not the quiet end of the choral repertoire. A church service can go further, because the setting carries it.

The judgement worth making early is whether the event is for clients or for staff. The two want different evenings, and firms that try to do both at once usually produce something that suits neither.


### Staff events, and why they are worth doing separately

The internal case for carol singing is different from the client case and often stronger. A firm where people work in silos gets very little from another email about Christmas; an hour of singing in the atrium at five o’clock pulls three floors into one space and costs less than the client event does.

What works is a lunchtime or end-of-day slot with no speeches attached. The moment anyone gives a talk it becomes an occasion people can decline. Sung carols with a song sheet for the last fifteen minutes is the format that gets the most people singing, and it is the part that comes back in engagement surveys.

Trainees and support staff often turn out in bigger numbers than partners, which is worth knowing when you choose the floor. Put the singers where the most people already are rather than where the most senior people sit.


### Budgets and how this gets approved

The figure is fixed and quoted in writing, which is the part that matters for anyone putting it through a procurement process. Prices include all taxes, fees and travel within Greater London, and there is no Christmas uplift: December is charged at the same rates as June.

Against the catering bill for a client drinks party, the music is a small line. A four-voice booking at £1,150 for 150 guests is under £8 a head.

We invoice the firm directly and can bill to a cost centre or a purchase order where your finance team needs that. We will also provide the paperwork most firms ask for before a supplier is set up.


### The December diary problem

Professional services firms have the same three weeks in their diaries as everyone else, and the middle two weeks of December are the tightest fortnight in our year. The Thursday before the last working week is the single most requested evening.

Most years our December dates are gone by the middle of September. Firms that hold an annual slot should rebook as soon as next year’s date is fixed, which for a lot of our clients means the week after this year’s event.

Later enquiries are always worth making, because the right combination of singers is sometimes still free. Send the date and we will confirm availability the same day. Our guide on when to book Christmas entertainment sets out how the month fills.


### What we need from you

The date, the building, the floor or room, the guest count, and whether the event is for clients or staff. If there are speeches, the running order and who is cueing the singers.

Photographs of the space are more useful than dimensions. What we are looking at is the floor surface, the ceiling height, and where the bar will be.

We deal with your facilities team and the building’s managing agent directly once the booking is confirmed, and send you the access and arrival times rather than asking you to relay them.


### Frequently asked questions


#### Where do carol singers perform in a City office?

The atrium, usually at the foot of a staircase or on a mezzanine, because those spaces are hard-surfaced with height and carry sound to several floors. A carpeted client-floor reception with a low ceiling is the hardest room, and either needs six voices or the singers moved to a stairwell.


#### Do we need permission from the building to have carol singers?

Usually, if you do not control the building. Singing in a shared atrium means clearing it with the managing agent as well as your own facilities team. The performance is unamplified with no power requirement and no stage, which is what the building will want to know.


#### Is live music worth it for a client Christmas party?

Against a catering bill it is a small line. Four voices at £1,150 for 150 guests is under £8 a head. Firms that book it tend to rebook the same evening annually until it becomes a fixture.


#### Should a firm run one Christmas event for clients and staff together?

They want different evenings. Client events call for all-black dress and close-harmony repertoire; staff events can be less formal and the feedback is better when they are. Firms that combine the two usually produce something that suits neither.

Summary: What the words of the best-known Christmas carols actually mean: the archaic phrases, the mistranslations, and the lines most people get wrong.

## Christmas carol lyrics and what they mean

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

Most people can sing three verses of half a dozen carols without having any idea what the words mean. The texts are old, several are translations, and a few of the most-sung lines mean close to the opposite of what they sound like. This guide goes through the phrases that puzzle people most.


### “God rest ye merry, gentlemen”

The comma is in the wrong place in almost every printed carol sheet, and moving it changes the sentence entirely. It is not addressed to merry gentlemen. Rest here means keep or make, and merry means strong or mighty rather than cheerful, so the line asks God to keep you strong, gentlemen.

The same sense of merry survives in “merry England” and in the archaic phrase “make merry”. It is the older meaning, and it is why the next line runs “let nothing you dismay” — the whole opening is a blessing against fear, not a greeting to a group of jolly men.

Printed correctly it should read: God rest ye merry, gentlemen . If your order of service has it as God rest ye, merry gentlemen , it is worth fixing before it goes to print.


### “Hark! The Herald Angels Sing”

Charles Wesley wrote “Hark, how all the welkin rings” in 1739. Welkin is an Old English word for the vault of the sky, so the original line has the whole heavens ringing. George Whitefield changed it to the version we sing, which is more singable and less interesting.

“Veiled in flesh the Godhead see” is the line that stops people. It is a compressed statement of the incarnation: divinity concealed inside a body. “Hail th’incarnate Deity” two lines later says the same thing again more plainly.

The tune has nothing to do with Christmas either. Mendelssohn wrote it in 1840 for a cantata celebrating the four hundredth anniversary of printing, and said he thought it would never suit sacred words. It was fitted to Wesley’s text after his death.


### “O Come, All Ye Faithful”

The Latin original, Adeste Fideles , is usually credited to John Francis Wade in the 1740s, though the authorship has been argued over for two centuries. The English translation most churches sing is Frederick Oakeley’s, from 1841.

“Very God, begotten not created” is not a claim that God is emphatic. Very here means true or actual, from the Latin verus , and the whole phrase is lifted from the Nicene Creed. It is a fourth-century doctrinal formula sitting in the middle of a Christmas carol.

“Lo, He abhors not the Virgin’s womb” is the line that most often gets quietly dropped from corporate carol sheets. It means he does not shrink from being born as a human being.


### “In the Bleak Midwinter”

Christina Rossetti wrote the poem around 1872 for an American magazine, and it was not intended as a carol at all. “Snow had fallen, snow on snow” is doing something specific: the repetition slows the line to the pace of the weather it describes.

“Heaven cannot hold Him, nor earth sustain” sets up the contrast the whole poem turns on — the immensity of the subject against a stable. The last verse, “What can I give Him, poor as I am?”, is the reason the poem endures; it is the only carol in common use that ends on a question about the singer rather than a statement about the child.

The midwinter itself is invention. Nobody knows the season, and a Judean December looks nothing like the frosty wind Rossetti describes. She was writing about an English winter and knew it.


### “Once in Royal David’s City”

Cecil Frances Alexander wrote the words in 1848 as part of a collection explaining the Apostles’ Creed to children, which is why the verses are so plainly constructed. Royal David’s city is Bethlehem, David’s birthplace.

“He came down to earth from heaven, who is God and Lord of all” is the creed line the verse was built to teach. The middle verses about the child being “mild, obedient, good as He” are Victorian schoolroom morality and are often cut now, which is a defensible edit.

The tradition of a solo treble singing the first verse unaccompanied at King’s College began in 1919, a year after the service itself. The chorister is not told in advance who will sing, which is a piece of theatre and also a kindness.


### “The Twelve Days of Christmas”

The twelve days run from Christmas Day to Epiphany on 6 January, not up to Christmas. The song is a cumulative memory game of French origin, first printed in English in 1780.

You will often be told each gift is a coded catechism for persecuted Catholics. There is no evidence for it; the claim first appears in the 1990s and has been thoroughly picked apart since. It is a good story and it is not true, which is worth knowing before repeating it in an introduction from the lectern.

The four calling birds were originally “colly birds” — colly meaning coal-black, so blackbirds. The five gold rings may be ring-necked pheasants, which would make the first seven gifts all birds.


### “Ding Dong! Merrily on High”

The tune is a sixteenth-century French dance, printed in 1589 in a manual on how to dance. The words are much later: George Ratcliffe Woodward wrote them in 1924, deliberately archaic.

“Gloria, Hosanna in excelsis” is the extended refrain everyone recognises, and it means “Glory, save us, in the highest”. Hosanna began as a plea and became an exclamation of praise, which is the reverse of what most people assume.

Woodward’s verses are full of invented archaism — “e’en so here below, below” — and were mock-antique when he wrote them. He was writing pastiche, and knew his audience would enjoy it.


### “Good King Wenceslas”

Wenceslas was a real tenth-century Duke of Bohemia, murdered by his brother and declared a king posthumously. The Feast of Stephen is 26 December, so this is a Boxing Day carol rather than a Christmas one.

The story of the page following in his master’s footsteps to keep warm is the point of the whole thing, and the last two lines state the moral outright: “ye who now will bless the poor, shall yourselves find blessing”.

The tune is a thirteenth-century spring carol, Tempus adest floridum , about flowers appearing in the meadows. J. M. Neale attached his winter text to it in 1853, which some Victorian critics thought was vandalism.


### “Silent Night”

Written in Austria in 1818, words by Joseph Mohr and tune by Franz Gruber, and first performed with a guitar because the church organ was out of action. The English translation is John Freeman Young’s, from 1859.

“Round yon Virgin Mother and Child” confuses people because it looks like a spelling mistake. Yon means over there, and the line means “around that mother and child”. The German original is plainer still.

It is the most translated carol there is, sung in over three hundred languages, and UNESCO lists it as intangible cultural heritage.


### Getting the words right on the night

Print every verse you intend to sing, at a size an older congregation can read. People sing the first verse from memory and go quiet in the second, and the usual cause is not shyness but a service sheet set in ten point.

Decide in advance which verses you are cutting. Most carols have verses that are routinely dropped, and a congregation half of whom are singing verse four while the choir has moved to verse five is a mess that takes two lines to recover from.

If someone is introducing the carols from the lectern, give them something true to say. A short, accurate note about where a text came from lands better than the twelve-days catechism story, and does not require anyone in the room to correct it afterwards.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What does “God rest ye merry, gentlemen” mean?

It asks God to keep you strong. Rest means keep or make, and merry means mighty rather than cheerful, so it is a blessing rather than a greeting. The comma belongs after merry, not before it, which most printed carol sheets get wrong.


#### What does “veiled in flesh the Godhead see” mean?

It is a compressed statement of the incarnation: divinity concealed inside a human body. The line comes from Charles Wesley's Hark! The Herald Angels Sing, and the next line, hail th'incarnate Deity, restates it more plainly.


#### When are the twelve days of Christmas?

From Christmas Day to Epiphany on 6 January, not the twelve days leading up to Christmas. The claim that each gift is a coded Catholic catechism has no evidence behind it and first appears in the 1990s.


#### Why is Good King Wenceslas sung at Christmas?

It is set on the Feast of Stephen, 26 December, so it is a Boxing Day carol. Wenceslas was a real tenth-century Duke of Bohemia, and the tune is a thirteenth-century spring carol about flowers, repurposed by J. M. Neale in 1853.

We sing carol services in churches, offices and livery halls across the UK, and Luca is happy to supply short, accurate notes on the texts for your order of service or for whoever is introducing them.

Source: https://londonchoralservice.com/music-guides/advent-carols-vs-christmas-carols.html
Summary: The difference between Advent and Christmas carols, which belongs before 25 December, and how to programme a service that sits in the weeks between.

## Advent carols vs Christmas carols

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Last updated: July 2026

Advent and Christmas are two different seasons with two different repertoires, and a fair number of December carol services mix them without meaning to. In a corporate setting nobody will complain. In a church, an incumbent may well have views, and it is easier to know the distinction before you build the programme than after.


### Two seasons, not one

Advent runs from the fourth Sunday before Christmas to Christmas Eve. Christmas begins on 25 December and runs twelve days to Epiphany. Almost every carol service held in the UK happens during Advent, which is the source of the confusion: people gather in Advent to sing Christmas carols.

Advent is a season of waiting and preparation. Its texts look forward — to a coming, to a promise not yet kept — and its music is correspondingly restrained, often modal and often in a minor key. Christmas texts announce that the thing has happened.

Liturgically the two are as distinct as Lent and Easter. In practice most December services blur them, and the pragmatic question is not whether to blur but how much.


### The Advent repertoire


#### O Come, O Come, Emmanuel

The Advent carol. The text is built from the O Antiphons, sung on the seven days before Christmas Eve, and the tune is a fifteenth-century French processional. Modal, unhurried, and entirely about waiting: “Rejoice! Emmanuel shall come to thee, O Israel” is future tense throughout.


#### Come, Thou Long Expected Jesus

Charles Wesley, and the title says the whole thing. Straightforwardly Advent and sung as a hymn more often than as a carol.


#### Lo, He Comes with Clouds Descending

Advent in its other mode. This is about the second coming and the last judgement, not the nativity, and it is a good deal more alarming than most people expect from a December hymn. Sung to Helmsley it is one of the grandest things in the English repertoire.


#### On Jordan’s Bank and Hills of the North, Rejoice

Both belong to the preparation theme: John the Baptist, and the summons to make ready. Neither mentions a stable.


#### Adam Lay Ybounden

Fifteenth-century, and properly Advent, because it is about the fall that made the incarnation necessary. Boris Ord’s setting is the one most choirs sing.


### The Christmas repertoire

Everything that describes the birth as having happened: O Come, All Ye Faithful , Hark! The Herald Angels Sing , Silent Night , Away in a Manger , In the Bleak Midwinter , O Little Town of Bethlehem .

Once in Royal David’s City is Christmas, though its use as the opening of Nine Lessons and Carols on Christmas Eve puts it right on the boundary.

Epiphany carols are a third category again and are routinely sung too early. We Three Kings belongs to 6 January, not to a service on 12 December, and the Wise Men do not arrive in the story until well after the shepherds have gone.


### Does it matter?

For a corporate carol service, a hotel lobby or a residents’ evening: no. Nobody is keeping liturgical time at a drinks reception, and a programme of Advent restraint would disappoint a room that came to hear Ding Dong! Merrily on High .

For a service in a church, it depends entirely on the incumbent. Some are relaxed; some hold the line firmly and will not have Christmas carols before the fourth Sunday of Advent. Ask early, because it is a decision that shapes the whole programme and it is not yours to make.

The middle position, which most parishes take, is an Advent carol service in early December that keeps some Advent material and admits the best-known Christmas carols at the end. That is a defensible shape and it satisfies almost everybody.


### Building a service that sits in Advent

An Advent carol service is a real form with its own shape: it moves from darkness towards light, both musically and often literally, with the church lit progressively as the service goes on. The readings run from the prophets through to the annunciation rather than to the nativity.

A workable programme opens with O Come, O Come, Emmanuel , keeps the middle in Advent territory with Adam Lay Ybounden , an O Antiphon setting and something from the Advent Prose, and finishes with one or two Christmas carols as the light comes up. Ending in Advent is possible and takes some nerve; a congregation that has waited an hour usually wants the arrival.

Our guide to carols by candlelight covers the lighting side, which matters more for an Advent service than for a Christmas one.


### The O Antiphons

Seven ancient texts sung at Vespers on 17 to 23 December, each addressing Christ by a different title: Wisdom, Lord, Root of Jesse, Key of David, Dayspring, King of Nations, Emmanuel. They are the source of O Come, O Come, Emmanuel , whose verses are the antiphons in metrical translation.

The initials of the Latin titles, read backwards, spell ero cras — “tomorrow I shall be”. Whether that was designed or noticed later is disputed, and it is a better piece of lectern material than most.

Choirs sometimes sing one antiphon as a choir-only item in an Advent service, which is the most direct way to put genuine Advent material into a programme that is otherwise heading for Christmas.


### Advent in a secular programme

Even where liturgy is irrelevant, the Advent repertoire is worth raiding for one practical reason: contrast. A programme of nine cheerful major-key Christmas carols flattens out. One modal Advent piece in the middle resets the room’s ear and makes the carol after it sound brighter than it would have on its own.

O Come, O Come, Emmanuel is the piece that does this best and needs no explanation to a secular audience, because most people know it without knowing what season it belongs to.

The same trick works with the darker traditional carols. The Coventry Carol is technically Christmas, being about the massacre of the innocents, but it does the same job of changing the temperature.


### Where the boundary actually falls in practice

The fourth Sunday of Advent is the point most parishes relax. Before it, Advent material and restraint; after it, Christmas carols are fair game because Christmas Eve is days away. A service on 20 December is treated very differently from one on 5 December, even in the same building.

Schools are the exception at the other end. A school carol service is usually held in the second week of December because term ends, and no school has ever moved its date on liturgical grounds. Everyone accepts that, including most clergy.

Cathedral and collegiate foundations tend to hold the line hardest, because they sing the full Advent liturgy anyway and a carol service is one item in a season rather than the whole of it.


### Telling the audience which is which

If your programme mixes the two, one sentence in the order of service does a lot of work: a note that the first half looks forward and the second half arrives. It turns what could read as muddle into a deliberate shape.

This also gives whoever is introducing the carols something worth saying. “This one is about waiting; the next one is about arriving” is a better line from the lectern than a summary of the plot.

For a corporate audience it is worth about thirty seconds and no more. The distinction is interesting and it is not what anybody came for.


### Common mistakes

Singing We Three Kings in Advent. Epiphany material at a December service is the most frequent slip and the one a clergy reader is most likely to notice.

Treating O Come, O Come, Emmanuel as a Christmas carol. It is the single most Advent thing in the repertoire, and putting it after the nativity reading reverses the story.

Assuming the incumbent will not mind. Ask. It costs one email and it avoids a conversation in the vestry twenty minutes before the service.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What is the difference between an Advent carol and a Christmas carol?

Advent carols look forward to a coming that has not yet happened and tend to be modal and restrained. Christmas carols announce the birth as an event that has occurred. O Come, O Come, Emmanuel is Advent; O Come, All Ye Faithful is Christmas.


#### Can you sing Christmas carols during Advent?

At a corporate event, hotel or residents' evening, yes, and nobody will mind. In a church it depends on the incumbent: some are relaxed, others will not have Christmas carols before the fourth Sunday of Advent. Ask before you build the programme.


#### When should We Three Kings be sung?

At Epiphany, 6 January, rather than at a December carol service. The Wise Men do not arrive in the narrative until well after the shepherds, and singing it in Advent is the slip a clergy reader is most likely to notice.


#### What are the O Antiphons?

Seven ancient texts sung at Vespers from 17 to 23 December, each addressing Christ by a different title. They are the source of the verses of O Come, O Come, Emmanuel, and the initials of the Latin titles read backwards spell ero cras, tomorrow I shall be.

We sing both Advent and Christmas services, and Luca will build a programme that fits whichever season your date actually falls in, including squaring it with the incumbent where that matters.

Summary: How to choose funeral singers in London: what to look for, ensemble sizes for crematoria and parish churches, 2026 price ranges, and questions to ask.

## Best funeral singers in London — what to look for

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 8 May 2026

Most families face this decision in a few days, often while still arranging the rest of the service, and almost always under the weight of a recent loss. This guide is a practical orientation: what to look for in funeral singers, how to match the size of the group to the size of the venue, what things cost in London in 2026, and the questions worth asking any provider before you book. London has a particular geography of funerals — large parish churches, smaller chapels of rest, and the major crematoria at Hendon, Golders Green, Honor Oak, and West London — and the right singers depend partly on which of those rooms you are in.


### What to look for

The first thing to look for is qualification. Funeral singing is real work: sight-reading hymns and anthems, holding a tune above an unfamiliar congregation, blending in four-part harmony with three colleagues, often in a difficult acoustic. The singers you want will be conservatoire-trained or cathedral-trained, with regular professional engagements outside funeral work. Ask. A good provider will tell you where their singers studied and what else they sing.

The second thing — less obvious, more important — is whether the musicians actually sing together as an ensemble. There is a real difference between a quartet who rehearse together every week and a quartet assembled from four diaries on a Tuesday for a Friday funeral. Both are technically a quartet, but only the first sounds like one. Ensemble cohesion is what makes a four-voice group fill a parish church; without it the sound is competent but thin.

Look at repertoire next. The standard funeral hymns are the floor, not the ceiling. The singers you want will be comfortable across the range — Anglican hymnody, Catholic Mass settings, the classical solo repertoire (Schubert, Fauré, Franck), and secular pieces a family might request: a Beatles song, a folk tune, something the person sang at home. If a provider has only the popular hymns, they cannot meet the request when it comes.

Then professionalism, which at a funeral means specific things. Singers who arrive 45 to 60 minutes early and check in with the funeral director. Singers who know to stand at the back, not the front, unless asked otherwise. Singers who do not chat in the porch as mourners arrive. Singers who, if a family member is overcome and cannot read, can step forward and read the lesson without making a thing of it. This last rarely comes up but it is worth knowing the people in the choir stalls could handle it if it did.

And discretion. Plain dark dress is the default. No social-media posting from the service. No introducing themselves to the family unless invited to. The job is to support what is happening in the room, not to be visible in it.

Two more practical points families often do not think to ask about. First, how the singers treat the order of service: it is the family’s document, and a good provider follows it as written, though in a Catholic Mass — where particular pieces belong at particular points — a knowledgeable music director will flag a misplacement before the day. Second, whether they bring their own folders and stands, or expect the venue to provide them. A small thing, but the difference between a tidy choir stall and a scattered one shows up in photographs the family will see for years.


### Ensemble size guidance

The right size depends on the venue and on what you want the music to do. The four common configurations:


#### Solo singer

A single trained voice singing one or two pieces — Pie Jesu, Ave Maria, Panis Angelicus, or a hymn the family wants sung rather than congregational. At a small service, particularly in a chapel of rest or a quiet crematorium slot, a soloist often fills the room more effectively than a larger ensemble, because a single voice leaves silence around it for the congregation to sit in.


#### Small Choir (4)

One voice on each of four parts — soprano, alto, tenor, bass. A quartet is the most useful configuration for almost every London funeral. It is large enough to lead the congregation in hymns and to sing four-part anthems with proper harmonic colour, and small enough to fit a crematorium chapel without crowding the family or to sit in a smaller parish church without dominating it. If you are unsure what to book, a quartet is almost always the answer.


#### Sextet

Six singers, usually two voices to a part on the upper voices and one each on tenor and bass, or some similar division. A sextet brings noticeably more weight than a quartet and works particularly well in larger parish churches with bigger naves — St Bride’s on Fleet Street, St Paul’s Knightsbridge, Southwark Cathedral. It is the right size when you expect a large congregation singing alongside the choir.


#### Full choir

Eight to twelve singers (or more). Reserved for memorial services with substantial congregations, civic funerals, and services in cathedrals or abbeys — Westminster Abbey, Southwark Cathedral, the larger Wren churches in the City. A full choir is rarely the right answer at a crematorium; the rooms at Honor Oak, Golders Green, Mortlake, and the rest are not built to hold the sound of twelve voices, and the family ends up sitting closer to the choir than to the coffin.

One useful test if you are unsure. Visit the venue, or ask the funeral director how many it seats. Under sixty seats, lean toward soloist or quartet. Sixty to two hundred, quartet is almost always right. Two hundred to four hundred and a parish-church acoustic, sextet. Larger than that, or a service with public attendance, full choir. The sound of an under-sized ensemble in a large room is thin; the sound of an over-sized ensemble in a small room is closer to overwhelming.


### Price ranges across the market in 2026

Indicative ranges for funeral singing in London this year. Variation within each range reflects ensemble seniority, complexity of repertoire, and the day and time of the service.

A reputable London provider’s fee will include rehearsal time, sheet music, a music director or fixer who handles communication with the funeral director and the church, and travel within Greater London. What pushes a quote toward the upper bound: bespoke arrangements (a piece transcribed or rearranged for the ensemble), late-notice booking inside seven days, and Saturday-morning slots at popular crematoria, which book out further ahead than weekday slots.

A quote well below the others is worth asking about rather than assuming the worst. Sometimes it means the singers are paid under the going rate, which tends to show up in the room. Sometimes it means the provider is not VAT-registered, or carries less overhead than an agency. Ask what the fee covers and the answer usually settles it.

A few notes on what is and is not standard within those ranges. An organist, where the venue does not provide one, is usually quoted separately and adds £200 to £350 depending on the music. A harpist or string player to accompany a soloist is similar. A music director who attends the service to direct the choir is included in our quotes for sextet and full choir, optional for a quartet. VAT is not normally charged by smaller providers; larger ones may add it. One London provider, The London Funeral Singers, publishes a price list showing £1,400 + VAT for four singers, or £1,680 including VAT. Always ask whether the figure you are looking at includes everything, or whether musicians’ expenses, music director, and travel are extras. The gap between an apparently cheaper quote and a transparent one often disappears once everything is on the page.


### Six questions to ask any provider

Before booking, it is reasonable to ask:

- Can the singers arrive 45 to 60 minutes early and check in with the funeral director?
- What if I want a particular hymn in a non-standard key for the congregation — can the singers transpose, or work from a transposition you provide?
- Do you carry sheet music for less-common pieces, or only the popular hymns and anthems?
- What is your replacement plan if a singer falls ill on the morning of the service?
- Can you accommodate a short-notice booking — less than seven days?
- Will the singers be in plain dark dress, in robes, or something else? (And does that match the venue?)
Any reputable provider will have a clear answer to all six. If a question gets a vague answer, push on it — a funeral is not the day to discover the replacement plan was “hope nothing happens.”

### Frequently asked questions

We can usually arrange singers within 48 hours for a funeral in London, and shorter notice is often possible. Our singers are based across the city and keep diary space for short-notice work, because most families are not booking weeks in advance.


#### Can singers learn an unfamiliar hymn at short notice?

Yes. Professional funeral singers read music and can prepare an unfamiliar hymn in a single rehearsal. If you have a piece in mind that is not in the standard repertoire, send the sheet music or a recording when you book and we will have it ready.


#### Should I have hymns or a soloist or both?

Most London funerals have at least one congregational hymn and one piece sung by the singers alone. Hymns give the room something to do together; a solo or choral piece gives the room a moment to sit and listen. Both serve different needs and most services benefit from having one of each.

A parish choir is the resident choir of a particular church and sings only at that church. The two are not in competition; in many parishes they sing together when the family wants both.
