## Best wedding choirs in London — what to look for

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford · Published May 2026

If you are getting married in London and want a choir to sing at the ceremony, you have a wider choice than in most cities — and that is part of the problem. The city has hundreds of trained singers passing through Royal Academy of Music, Royal College of Music, Guildhall, and Trinity Laban each year, parish choirs at every level, and a long tail of agency listings on Encore, Alive Network, and PopTop that flatten quality and price into a single grid. This guide is for couples and wedding planners trying to make a sensible choice. It covers what training and experience to look for, how to match ensemble size to venue, what realistic 2026 prices look like across the market, and the six questions worth asking any provider before you book.


### What to look for in a wedding choir

The single biggest variable in wedding-choir quality is whether the singers have been trained in the choral tradition. A graduate ensemble drawn from the Royal Academy of Music, the Royal College of Music, the Guildhall School, Trinity Laban, the Royal Northern College of Music, or the choral foundations of Oxford and Cambridge will read sight-unseen, blend without coaching, and tune chords cleanly in a live acoustic. A parish choir with willing amateurs will not, however well-meaning the singers are. Both are valid choices for the right wedding; they are not the same product, and they should not cost the same.

Repertoire breadth matters more than couples expect. A ceremony usually wants a sacred choral piece for the entrance or signing of the register, two or three congregational hymns, perhaps a secular art song, and increasingly a pop arrangement somewhere in the service. A choir that lives entirely inside the Anglican service tradition will be wonderful at the hymns and Stanford anthems and out of its depth in a Sondheim setting. A choir that lives entirely in pop arrangements will be the opposite. Ask for a sample programme of recent weddings rather than a polished showcase — the spread tells you what they actually do.

The other thing worth checking is whether the singers regularly work together. Some London ensembles are fixed groups that rehearse weekly through the year. Others are fixers who book a different four singers for each gig from a shared pool. The latter can deliver a fine sound if the personnel are strong, but the blend and the visual cohesion will not match a settled ensemble. For a wedding, where the choir stands in front of every guest for an hour, that distinction is audible and visible.

Professionalism on the day is the part that does not show up on a website. Singers who arrive in matching dress, half an hour before guests start arriving, with their music already learned, are the difference between a service that runs on rails and one that does not. Ask whether the choir provides its own folders, whether the music director is included in the fee, and how they handle the practicalities of a ten-minute window between the previous wedding and yours.

References and recordings are non-negotiable. A polished studio recording proves a choir can sound good with multiple takes and post-production; it does not prove they can deliver a service live. Ask for an unedited recording from a recent wedding — ideally one shot on a phone from the back of a church. If a provider cannot produce one, ask why.


### Ensemble size guidance

Match the choir to the room. The acoustic of a London ceremony venue does most of the work; oversizing the ensemble is the most common and most expensive mistake couples make.

For the largest spaces — Westminster Abbey, St Bride’s Fleet Street, St Paul’s Knightsbridge, the Temple Church — a sextet is the practical minimum for a confident sound, and an eight- to twelve-voice ensemble starts to feel proportionate to the architecture. Below a sextet, the voices do not carry and the choir reads as decorative rather than musical. These are buildings designed for choral foundations of twenty or more, and the music written for them assumes that.

For mid-sized London churches and chapels — the Brompton Oratory, Chelsea Old Church, Holy Trinity Sloane Square, St Mary’s Bourne Street, the Guards’ Chapel — a quartet to sextet is usually right. A quartet of strong soloists can hold one of these rooms if the singers are first-rate; a sextet adds depth at the bottom and confidence in congregational hymns. Country house chapels with a hundred or so guests fall into this band too.

Smaller City churches, registry offices, and intimate ceremonies of forty or fifty guests do not need more than a quartet, and a single strong soloist will often carry the ceremony on their own. At Old Marylebone Town Hall or Chelsea Town Hall the room itself is acoustically dry, and a small ensemble singing close to the couple will read better than a larger one fighting the architecture. For garden ceremonies and marquees, treat any voice count as a chamber-music decision rather than a choral one — a quartet at most, and it should be one chosen for clean blend rather than weight.

For reception singing — singers wandering through canapés — you do not want a full choir. One or two confident soloists with a guitar or a pianist behind them will work the room rather than perform at it; if you would rather have no instrument at all, take a quartet, because two voices on their own run out of harmony fast. This is a different skillset, and not every classical ensemble does it well; ask specifically.


### Price ranges across the market in 2026

Wedding-choir prices in London cluster into clear bands once you control for training and ensemble cohesion. Directory marketplaces (Encore Musicians, Alive Network, PopTop, Bark) flatten these ranges and obscure what drives them, so it is worth knowing the shape of the market before you start comparing quotes.

A single trained singer for one ceremony piece — the bride entering to a Schubert Ave Maria, for example — sits at £200 to £300. A quartet, the workhorse size for most London weddings, ranges from £900 to £1,400 depending on whether the singers are conservatoire graduates and whether the ensemble rehearses regularly. A sextet is typically £1,400 to £2,000. A full choir of eight to twelve or more voices for a large church wedding sits between £2,000 and £3,500, and can run higher for cathedral-scale services with custom arrangements.

What drives price within these bands is straightforward. Rehearsal time costs money: a fixed ensemble that rehearses weekly through the year carries a higher per-singer rate than a pickup group assembled the week before. Travel inside the M25 is usually included; outside it adds a per-singer travel fee. Custom arrangements — a four-part setting of a pop song the couple have chosen — cost between £150 and £400 to commission, on top of the ensemble fee. A separate soloist for a processional aria, sung over the choir, adds £200 to £400. A music director who attends the rehearsal and conducts on the day is included in some packages and charged separately in others; ask.

The lowest quotes on directory sites are almost always pickup groups of mixed training. The highest quotes are usually fixed conservatoire ensembles with custom-arranged repertoire and a music director. Both can be the right choice; they are not equivalent, and the gap between the two is real.


### Six questions to ask any provider

The quickest way to separate a serious provider from a marketplace listing is to ask six concrete questions. The answers, and how readily they come, tell you most of what you need to know.

- What is the training and conservatoire background of the singers I would be hiring? A good provider will name the institutions and, for a higher-end booking, name the singers. A vague answer is itself an answer.
- Can I hear an unedited recording from a recent wedding — not a polished album? Phone recordings from the back of a church are far more revealing than a studio demo. If they cannot share one, ask why.
- Is the ensemble fixed, or are singers booked per gig from a pool? Both models exist, and both can work, but they produce different products. You should know which one you are paying for.
- What does your fee include — rehearsals, travel, music director, sheet music, custom arrangements? The headline price often excludes things that turn out to be essential. Get the inclusions in writing.
- Can you take a custom arrangement of a song we would like sung? If yes, ask the lead time and the additional cost. If no, ask which existing arrangements they hold for that style of song.
- What is your contingency if a key singer falls ill the day before? A serious provider has a deps list and a process. A pickup group may not. The day before the wedding is not the time to find out.

### Frequently asked questions


#### Should I hire a choir or just a soloist for our wedding?

A soloist is enough if you want a single processional aria or a piece during the signing of the register. A choir earns its place when you have congregational hymns to lead, when the venue is large enough that one voice will not fill it, or when you want harmonised settings rather than melody and accompaniment.


#### How early should I book a wedding choir for a London wedding?

Twelve to eighteen months ahead is normal for a Saturday in May, June, or September at a well-known London church. For weekday weddings or off-peak dates, three to six months is usually enough. The strongest fixed ensembles book up first, so the earlier you enquire the more choice you have.


#### Can a choir sing pop songs as well as classical?

Yes, but it depends on the arrangement. A four-part choral arrangement of a pop song needs to exist on the page before the rehearsal — choirs cannot improvise harmony to a pop tune the way a band can. Ask whether the provider has its own arrangements, can commission one for you, or holds a library of existing wedding-friendly settings.


#### Is amplification needed in a large church?

Almost never for a trained choir. Stone churches with reverberant acoustics — Westminster Abbey, St Paul’s Knightsbridge, the Brompton Oratory — were built to carry unamplified voices. Amplification is mostly relevant for civil ceremonies in dry rooms, marquees, and outdoor weddings.


#### Do London wedding choirs travel outside London?

Most do. London-based ensembles regularly perform at country house weddings in the Home Counties and further afield. Expect a travel fee for venues outside the M25, and an overnight allowance for ceremonies more than around two hours from central London.

Source: https://londonchoralservice.com/music-guides/ubi-caritas-wedding.html
Summary: Ubi Caritas is one of the few sacred texts whose subject is love. Why Ola Gjeilo's setting suits a wedding, where to place it, and how many singers it needs.

## Ubi Caritas at a wedding — Ola Gjeilo’s setting

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 15 August 2026

Most wedding music is about love by association. Ubi Caritas is about love outright: the Latin says that where charity and love are, God is there. Ola Gjeilo’s setting is the modern choral piece couples ask us for most, and the first one we suggest when a couple has run out of ideas for the register signing.

Our choir singing Ubi Caritas by Ola Gjeilo. Hear more recordings .


### The text is about love, and about little else

The standard wedding repertoire is mostly about something else. Schubert’s Ave Maria is a prayer to the Virgin. Panis Angelicus is about the Eucharist. Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring is a chorale about faith. All three are beautiful, and all three are borrowed. They get used at weddings because they sound right; marriage is not what any of them is about.

Ubi Caritas is the exception. The antiphon is sung on Maundy Thursday during the washing of feet, and its opening line is the whole argument: Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est — where charity and love are, God is there. Then comes the line that does the real work at a wedding: Congregavit nos in unum Christi amor , love has gathered us together into one. That is a description of the room. A hundred and twenty people who would otherwise never be in a building together have been assembled by two people’s affection for each other, and the piece names it while they sit there.

If you are not religious, you may worry that a Latin sacred text will feel imposed on your guests. Print the translation in the order of service and it reads as the plainest statement of the day’s purpose anyone will hear, including the address.


### Gjeilo’s setting, and how it differs from Duruflé’s

Two settings of this text are in regular use. Maurice Duruflé wrote his in 1960, as the first of his Quatre motets sur des thèmes grégoriens . It keeps the plainsong intact and wraps modal harmony around it, lasts about two minutes, and ends where it started. Ola Gjeilo, a Norwegian composer then in his early twenties, wrote his in 2001 from the same chant.

Duruflé stays quiet throughout: austere, restrained, and best in a building with a long acoustic and an audience that already listens to choral music. Gjeilo states the chant plainly, then divides the voices and lets the harmony thicken underneath it until the piece opens out into a full climax before settling back down to close. It has a shape guests can follow without knowing anything about plainsong.

That swell in the middle is why we suggest Gjeilo for weddings and Duruflé for quieter occasions. A guest who has sat through two hymns and a reading will follow a piece that goes somewhere further than one holding a single mood. Both are unaccompanied and both use the same chant, so you can put them side by side and hear the difference in about ninety seconds.

One practical note: Gjeilo’s setting is still in copyright, so a choir needs bought copies rather than photocopies. We deal with that as part of the booking.


### It runs about three minutes, which covers the heart of the register signing

Signing the register takes two to four minutes in most churches, depending on how many photographs the registrar allows and how slowly your witnesses write. Gjeilo’s Ubi Caritas runs to roughly three minutes, and it has a proper ending, so nobody has to fade it out or vamp until the pens go down.

It is a duller reason than the text, and it is why couples keep booking it. A great many beautiful choral works are the wrong length for the moment you want them in. Mozart’s Ave Verum Corpus runs to three minutes too, which is why it turns up at the same point in so many services. Anything much shorter leaves a gap; anything much longer and the choir is still singing while the wedding party stands about waiting to process out.

If your signing is likely to run long, pair it with an organ meditation afterwards rather than choosing a longer choral piece. For the full sequence of musical moments in a ceremony, our guide to wedding ceremony music walks through it from prelude to recessional.


### It needs no organ, and four singers will do

Ubi Caritas is unaccompanied. That makes it one of the few pieces of this quality you can have in a building with no organ, a bad organ, or an organ nobody has tuned since 2009 — which covers a fair number of the country houses, barns, and school chapels where people now get married.

Four singers can sing it, one voice to a part, and it works. Five or more makes a real difference: the music divides the voices at its fullest points, and the extra singers cover those divisions instead of leaving them folded back into the line. With eight in a resonant church you get the full spread of the chords. See our pricing for what each size of ensemble costs.

Acoustics matter more here than with a hymn. Unaccompanied voices need something to sing into: a stone church, or a hall with a high ceiling. Outdoors the sound has nothing to reflect off and the piece thins out, so we would add singers or suggest something else for an open-air ceremony.


### Where to place it in the ceremony

The signing of the register is the obvious home for it, and the one we recommend first. The congregation is seated, the couple are occupied, and there is a defined stretch of time for the piece to fill.

At a nuptial Mass it also works during communion, where its length and its stillness suit a queue of people moving quietly. Some couples put it immediately after the vows instead, as a few minutes of held breath before the service carries on; that placement lands harder and carries more risk, because it depends on the vows finishing when the order of service says they will.

We would not use it for the processional or the recessional. It has no pulse to walk to, and asking someone to time their entrance to a piece with no beat is unkind to everyone involved. Keep the organ for those, or see our guide to the best organ pieces for a wedding .


### If your ceremony is not in a church

A civil ceremony on approved premises in England and Wales — a hotel, a country house, a registry office — must be free of religious content, and the registrar will ask to see your readings and music in advance. This catches couples out. Ubi Caritas is in Latin, but registrars go by what the words mean, and the text names both God and Christ. It will not be approved.

That does not rule the piece out of your day. Have it at the drinks reception, during the wedding breakfast, or at a blessing held after the civil formalities, where nobody is checking. Several of our couples do this: the registrar gets a string quartet, and the choir sings Ubi Caritas twenty minutes later with a glass of champagne in every guest’s hand.

If the whole ceremony is secular, our list of pop songs for a wedding choir covers what a choir can sing instead.


### It is just as popular at funerals

The same qualities that suit a wedding — unaccompanied, about three minutes, a text about love rather than doctrine — make Ubi Caritas one of the pieces families ask for most at funerals and memorial services. Most place it at the entry of the coffin or as a reflection after the eulogy. Our guide to choosing funeral music covers where it fits alongside hymns.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What does Ubi Caritas mean?

Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est is Latin for “Where charity and love are, God is there.” The words come from an antiphon sung on Maundy Thursday during the washing of feet.


#### How long is Ola Gjeilo’s Ubi Caritas?

About three minutes; the signing itself usually takes five to ten, and the organ can cover the remainder.


#### How many singers does Ubi Caritas need?

Four is enough, with one voice to each part. Five or more makes a real difference, because the music divides the voices at its fullest points and the extra singers cover those divisions instead of leaving them folded back into the line.


#### Can we have Ubi Caritas at a civil ceremony?

Not during a civil ceremony on approved premises in England and Wales. The text names God and Christ, and the ceremony itself has to be free of religious content. You can have it at the drinks reception or the wedding breakfast instead.

Summary: A humanist wedding is wholly non-religious. The secular choral repertoire a choir can sing at one, where to place it, and the pieces that catch couples out.

## Choral music for a humanist wedding

By Luca Wetherall, Artistic Director & Tutor in Music, University of Oxford

Published 29 August 2026

A humanist wedding is a wholly non-religious ceremony, and most of the wedding choral repertoire is sacred. Take away the Ave Marias, the Panis Angelicus, and the settings of Ubi Caritas, and couples assume a choir has nothing left to sing. What is left is the secular part-song tradition: Stanford, Elgar, Vaughan Williams, Lauridsen, Whitacre, and four centuries of choral music about love, weather, and landscape with no God in it anywhere. Almost none of it gets sung at weddings, because church weddings have hymn books instead.


### What a humanist ceremony is

A humanist wedding is led by a celebrant accredited by Humanists UK or Humanist Society Scotland, and it is built around the couple rather than around a liturgy. There is no set form of words, no prayers, and no hymns. The celebrant writes the ceremony with you from scratch, usually over two or three long conversations, and the script is unique to you. Most run between twenty and thirty-five minutes.

In England and Wales the ceremony carries no legal force. Couples complete the legal formalities separately at a register office — a short appointment, often on a weekday, with two witnesses — and treat the humanist ceremony as the real wedding. In Scotland, Northern Ireland, Jersey, and Guernsey humanist marriages are legally recognised and no second ceremony is needed. Scotland recognised them in 2005, and since 2022 more humanist weddings have been conducted there each year than religious marriages of all denominations combined.

The Government announced in October 2025 that it intends to recognise humanist marriages in England and Wales as part of a wider reform of marriage law, and set out its proposals for consultation in July 2026. Its own projections suggest one in five couples would choose a humanist ceremony once the law changes. No date has been set, so if you are marrying in 2027 you should plan around the rules as they stand.


### Nobody is going to vet your music

Couples usually have this backwards. At a civil ceremony on approved premises — a hotel, a country house, a register office — the registrar has a duty to keep religious content out of the proceedings, and will ask to see your readings and your music in advance. People get told no. A Latin motet with God in the text will not be approved, whatever the guests take it to mean.

A humanist ceremony has no registrar in the room, because it is not the legal ceremony. Nobody signs off your programme. If you wanted Schubert’s Ave Maria at a humanist wedding, no authority exists to stop you; the constraint is your own conviction and your celebrant’s. Humanists UK celebrants conduct ceremonies without acts of worship, so a hymn or a prayer is out. A piece of music with a religious text sits in between, and it is a conversation with your celebrant rather than a rule handed down.

In practice almost every couple who chooses a humanist ceremony wants music that matches it. So the question worth asking is which pieces sound like your ceremony.


### The five minutes you have to build yourself

A church wedding has a hole in it made for a choir. The couple go off to sign the register with the vicar and two witnesses, the photographs are taken, and a hundred guests sit for four or five minutes with nothing to look at. That is where the anthem goes. A great deal of the wedding choral repertoire is the length it is because of that gap.

A humanist ceremony in England or Wales has no register to sign, because the signing happened at the register office weeks earlier. Remove it and the ceremony runs from processional to recessional with no built-in pause, which leaves a choir singing two pieces of walking music and nothing in between. We have had couples book six singers and then find there was nowhere to put them.

The answer is to build the moment on purpose. Three things do the job:

- A symbolic ritual with music underneath it. Handfasting takes three or four minutes done properly, and it is quiet work — hands bound with cord while the celebrant speaks or says nothing at all. A piece sung through it fills the time and covers the business with the ribbon. Ring warming, where the rings are passed around the guests before the exchange, takes longer still and needs music more.
- A keepsake certificate to sign. Many celebrants provide a commemorative certificate for the couple and their witnesses to sign during the ceremony. It has no legal weight and it restores the four-minute gap exactly.
- A stated listening moment. The celebrant says that the couple have chosen a piece of music and asks everyone to sit and hear it. This reads as artificial on paper. In the room it works, because guests who are told to listen do.
Any of the three gives the choir somewhere to sing something substantial, which is the difference between hiring singers and hiring bookends.


### English part-songs

Between roughly 1890 and 1930 English composers wrote a large body of unaccompanied secular music for choirs. It was written for competition festivals and choral societies rather than for churches, so it sits outside the sacred repertoire altogether, and hardly any of it is heard at weddings. This is the richest seam available to a humanist ceremony, and the least mined.


#### The Blue Bird (Stanford, 1910)

Mary Coleridge’s poem is eight lines about a bird crossing a lake. Stanford sets it for four parts held almost motionless while a solo soprano floats above them on the word “blue”. Three minutes, and one of the most beautiful things in the English repertoire. Nothing happens in it, which is exactly why it suits a handfasting: it holds one still image for as long as the ritual takes.


#### There Is Sweet Music (Elgar, 1907)

Tennyson, set for two choirs a semitone apart — the men in G, the women in A flat. That sounds like a stunt and produces a warm blur of sound instead. Four minutes. You want at least eight singers and a room with some resonance in it.


#### My Love Dwelt in a Northern Land (Elgar, 1889)

Andrew Lang’s poem, four voices, three minutes, and a love song without qualification. One of Elgar’s earliest published successes, written a decade before the Enigma Variations made his name.


#### The Turtle Dove (Vaughan Williams, 1919)

A folk song about a man leaving his love, arranged for a baritone soloist over a humming choir. The tune carries the piece and every guest will follow it. Two and a half minutes, and four singers are enough.


### Folk arrangements

Folk song is the safest ground at a humanist ceremony. The texts are about people rather than doctrine, the tunes are singable, and a guest who has never sat through a choral concert in their life will still follow one. These also travel better outdoors than anything else on this page.

Down by the Salley Gardens sets Yeats and has been arranged for choirs many times over; two minutes, and the melody does the work. The Water Is Wide is the one couples recognise, usually in Norman Luboff’s arrangement, and it walks well enough to serve as a processional. My Love Is Like a Red, Red Rose gives you Burns, which is useful if either family is Scottish. Loch Lomond in Vaughan Williams’s arrangement is a proper piece of writing rather than a singalong, with the caveat that he set it for a baritone soloist and men’s voices, so it needs the lower half of a larger group or a different arrangement altogether.

One to read before you choose: She Moved Through the Fair is as lovely as anything here, and in the last verse the woman returns as a ghost. Choirs routinely drop that verse. Ask whether yours is going to.


### Modern secular choral music

The living composers whose work fills wedding shortlists write a great deal of sacred music, and a smaller amount of secular music that couples never find because it is filed under concert repertoire.


#### Dirait-on (Lauridsen, 1993)

The last of Lauridsen’s Les Chansons des Roses , setting Rilke’s French poems about roses. Lauridsen wrote it as a folk song of his own invention, and it behaves like one: a tune that comes round again and gathers voices each time. Three and a half minutes. There is no religion anywhere in Rilke’s roses, which makes this the single most useful piece on this page.


#### The Seal Lullaby (Whitacre, 2004)

Kipling, from The Jungle Book — a mother seal singing her pup to sleep. Whitacre wrote it for an animated film that was never made. Three minutes, gentle, and it asks nothing difficult of the singers, which matters when you are booking four or six rather than twenty.


#### Sleep (Whitacre, 2000)

Written on Robert Frost’s Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening , then stripped of its text when the Frost estate refused permission; Charles Anthony Silvestri wrote new words to fit the existing music. Five minutes, and it needs eight voices or more to hold the chords open.


#### Tundra (Ola Gjeilo)

If you have heard Gjeilo’s Ubi Caritas at a friend’s wedding and wanted that sound without the Latin prayer, this is where to go. Silvestri’s words describe the Norwegian mountain plateau — grass, snow, sky, and nothing else. Same composer, same warmth, no God.


#### Sure on This Shining Night (Barber, or Lauridsen)

James Agee’s poem about a summer night and being alive underneath it. Barber wrote it as a solo song in 1938 and made the choral version later; Lauridsen set the same words again in 2005. Three minutes either way. The Barber is the more direct of the two and the easier to bring off with a small group.


#### This Marriage (Whitacre, 2004)

Worth raising because it is the one modern choral piece actually written about a marriage rather than borrowed for one — Whitacre wrote it for his own wedding anniversary, on Coleman Barks’s translation of Rumi. The text is a thirteenth-century Sufi poet’s: it asks that the marriage be blessed, and it mentions paradise and “here and hereafter”. Some humanist couples read that as poetry and take it. Others do not. Put it to your celebrant rather than deciding on your own.


### Madrigals, for guests arriving

The madrigal repertoire is secular by definition. The sixteenth century wrote its sacred music in Latin for church and its secular music in English or Italian for private houses, and the two never met. Morley’s Now Is the Month of Maying and April Is in My Mistress’ Face , Farmer’s Fair Phyllis , and Monteverdi’s Italian books are short, quick, and concerned with spring and courtship.

They were also written to be sung by five or six people standing in a room, which is precisely what a barn or a garden gives you. A long, slow, modern piece needs an acoustic to bloom in. A madrigal does not, and it holds up as background music while guests find their seats in a way a sustained chord never will.

Read the texts first. A fair number of madrigals are considerably filthier than their tunes let on.


### Pop songs, and one warning

Everything in our guide to pop songs for a wedding choir applies here, and applies more freely, since no registrar is deciding whether a lyric counts as religious. Close-harmony arrangements of the songs a couple already share are the most common request we get for humanist ceremonies, and a recessional that guests recognise sends everyone out of the room in the right mood.

The warning concerns Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah , which is requested for weddings more than any other single song. It contains King David, Bathsheba, Samson and Delilah, and the word itself several dozen times, so it is a strange fit for a ceremony chosen for its absence of religion. It is also, read closely, a song about a love that has already failed. We will sing it if you want it. We would rather tell you first.


### The pieces that catch couples out

Several standards feel secular and are not. Each of these reaches us on shortlists from couples who chose a humanist ceremony precisely because they are not religious.

- Ave Maria — a prayer to the Virgin Mary in the Schubert, the Bach–Gounod, and the Caccini. Schubert’s own text was Walter Scott’s, from The Lady of the Lake , and is not a prayer at all; the Latin was fitted to the tune afterwards. If it is the melody you love, it can be sung to Scott’s English or played without words.
- Panis Angelicus — a Eucharistic hymn. The subject is the bread of the Mass.
- Ubi Caritas — the antiphon says that where charity and love are, God is there. It is the finest wedding motet we sing and it names God in its first line. We have written about where it does belong .
- The Lord Bless You and Keep You — Rutter’s setting of a blessing from the Book of Numbers, and one of the most requested recessionals in the country.
- Pie Jesu , Jerusalem , For the Beauty of the Earth , Amazing Grace — prayers and hymns, all four, and all regularly asked for.
The inversion is worth knowing too. Wagner’s Bridal Chorus comes from Lohengrin , an opera, and Mendelssohn’s Wedding March was written for a production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Neither contains a religious word. Several Catholic dioceses will not allow the Wagner in their churches, so a humanist ceremony is in the odd position of being free to use the two most recognisable pieces of wedding music ever written, while a cathedral is not.


### No organ, and often no roof

Humanist ceremonies happen wherever the couple likes: gardens, barns, woodland, village halls, the family house, the top of a hill. None of it needs a licence, because licensing attaches to the legal ceremony and there isn’t one. That freedom is why people choose a humanist wedding, and it is the hardest part of the music.

Almost none of these venues has an organ, and plenty have no piano worth playing. Everything on this page is unaccompanied for that reason. Singers need no instrument, no power supply, and no tuning, and they take about a square metre each.

Outdoors is a separate problem. Unaccompanied voices need a surface to reflect from, and a lawn has none: the sound goes up and does not come back. Slow chord-based writing suffers most — Whitacre’s held harmonies depend on a room, and in the open air they thin out to nothing. Music with a strong tune and a clear pulse survives. The folk arrangements work outside. The madrigals work outside. Stanford’s Blue Bird, with a solo soprano over a hushed four-part accompaniment, does not, and we will say so rather than take the booking and let it fail on the day.

Two rules for an outdoor ceremony: add singers, and put them close. Six voices outside carry about as far as four inside. Standing the choir two metres behind the couple rather than off to one side means the back row hears something. If there is a marquee, sing inside it — canvas reflects far better than grass. See our pricing for what each size of ensemble costs.


### A worked programme

A thirty-minute humanist ceremony, six singers, no instruments:

- Guests arriving, fifteen minutes — madrigals. Morley’s Now Is the Month of Maying , Farmer’s Fair Phyllis , and three or four more. Short pieces, light on their feet. Nobody is listening properly yet, and that is fine.
- Processional — The Water Is Wide , or the Mendelssohn if you want the grin of recognition. Something with a pulse, because a person has to walk to it.
- The welcome and the readings — nothing. Let the celebrant work.
- Under the handfasting, three to four minutes — The Blue Bird indoors, The Turtle Dove outdoors.
- After the vows and the rings — Dirait-on . This is the emotional peak of the ceremony and it should get the best piece you have.
- Recessional — something fast and loud that the guests know.
That comes to six pieces, which is what six singers can hold to a professional standard on a single rehearsal. Asking for twelve is where wedding music programmes start to come apart. For the full shape of a ceremony from prelude to recessional, our guide to wedding ceremony music covers the church version alongside this one.


### Frequently asked questions


#### What music can you have at a humanist wedding?

Any music without religious content. There is no approved list and no registrar to clear it with, because a humanist ceremony in England and Wales is not the legal marriage. The secular choral repertoire covers English part-songs such as Stanford’s The Blue Bird, folk arrangements such as The Turtle Dove, Renaissance madrigals, and modern pieces such as Lauridsen’s Dirait-on and Whitacre’s The Seal Lullaby.


#### Can you have hymns at a humanist wedding?

No. Humanist celebrants conduct ceremonies without acts of worship, so hymns, prayers, and blessings are out. A piece of music with a religious text sits somewhere in between, and it is worth raising with your celebrant rather than assuming the answer either way.


#### Do you need a choir for a humanist wedding?

No, but humanist ceremonies are usually held in venues with no organ and often no usable piano, so unaccompanied singers are the practical way to have live music. Four singers cost from £1,150 and six from £1,600.


#### Is a humanist wedding legally binding in England and Wales?

Not at present. Couples in England and Wales complete the legal formalities separately at a register office. Humanist marriages are already legally recognised in Scotland, Northern Ireland, Jersey, and Guernsey. The Government set out proposals to recognise them in England and Wales in July 2026, but no date has been set.


#### Can a choir sing outdoors at a humanist ceremony?

Yes, with two adjustments. Unaccompanied voices have nothing to reflect off outdoors, so add singers and stand them close to the guests: six outside carry about as far as four inside. Music with a strong tune and a clear pulse survives; slow chord-based pieces that depend on a room’s resonance do not.


### Talk to us about your ceremony

Tell us where you are getting married and we will tell you what will work in the space. If it is outdoors we will say how many singers it needs. If the piece you have in your head turns out to have a God in it, we will find you the secular equivalent rather than try to talk you out of the ceremony you have planned. The conversation is free and there is no obligation.

Summary: Frequently asked questions about hiring The London Choral Service: travel beyond London, payment and deposits, repertoire, and instruments provided.

## Frequently asked questions

Answers to what people ask before booking singers, choirs, and musicians for a wedding, funeral, or corporate event.

These aren't specific to any one occasion. For specifics on yours, see weddings , funerals , corporate events , or Christmas carol services .


### Do you travel outside London?

Yes. London is our base, but we perform across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, and several of our singers live outside the capital, which helps keep travel costs down further afield. Prices on this site cover venues within Greater London; anywhere beyond that, we quote the travel cost before you book. Our area pages list the cities where we perform most often.


### Can we hear the choir before we book?

Yes. Our listen page has recordings of the hymns, songs, and instrumental pieces clients request most often, performed by the same musicians you would book. It's the easiest way to hear the sound of a soloist, a small choir, or a full ensemble before you commit.


### Can you help us choose the right music?

Yes. Tell us about the occasion, the venue, and any music that matters to you or your family, and we'll recommend pieces to match, along with a written quote setting out the ensemble and repertoire. Our music guides cover the pieces most requested for weddings, funerals, and Christmas services, if you would like to browse first.


### Can you provide an organist, pianist, or harpist as well as singers?

Yes. Alongside our singers, we provide organists, pianists, harpists, and string players, either accompanying a choir or performing on their own. An organist or pianist starts from £250 solo, or £225 added to a choir you've already booked; harpists and string players are quoted the same way, chosen to match your venue and repertoire. If a venue has no organ or piano, we bring a portable keyboard.


### How does payment work, and do you need a deposit?

It depends on the occasion. For weddings, we ask for a 30 per cent deposit at booking, with the balance due 14 days before the day. For funerals, given the short notice most families are working with, we invoice after the service instead, on 14-day terms. Corporate and business bookings are usually invoiced against a purchase order on standard 30-day terms, though we can issue an advance deposit invoice if your budget needs it that way. Ask when you enquire and we will confirm exactly how it works for your booking.


### How much space does the choir need?

Very little. Four to eight singers can perform from a corner of a room or the width of a small stage, with no risers or special staging required. If you would like instrumental accompaniment and the venue has no piano or organ, we bring a portable keyboard, which needs a standard socket within ten metres. Tell us about the room or venue when you enquire and we will confirm what fits.


### Can you perform outdoors?

Yes, for weddings, memorials, corporate events, and carol bookings alike. Gardens, courtyards, marquees, and woodland venues are all places we perform regularly. A full choir carries well in the open air; a soloist or a smaller group can get lost in a large or windy space, so we talk through the venue with you beforehand and bring discreet amplification if it would help.


### Can the choir sing in Latin or other languages?

Yes. Latin repertoire is a regular part of what we sing: pieces like Ave Maria, Ave Verum Corpus, Ubi Caritas, and Anima Christi come up often at both weddings and funerals. Our singers can also learn repertoire in other languages on request; let us know when you enquire and we will confirm what is possible for your programme.


### What happens if one of your singers is ill on the day?

If a singer falls ill we cover the part from within the team, with someone who already knows the repertoire before the day. This applies whatever the occasion; your booking is not cancelled for reasons on our side.

If your question isn't covered here, get in touch and we'll answer it directly.
